chapters.title: Authorisation and Distribution
chapters.purpose: Authorises the SSMM for use on all ships fully managed by WSM, DWM, WASM and Barber Ship Management Germany, and defines how the manual is distributed and controlled.
key_requirements: SSMM is authorised for use on board all ships fully managed by WSM, DWM, WASM and Barber Ship Management Germany.
Manual addresses safety and environment protection as required by the ISM Code, applicable ISO standards and the Company.
Master and all officers shall acquaint themselves with and comply with the contents applicable to their vessel type and with the Company Environmental Management System (EMS).
Officers may read operations for other vessel types for information only and must not confuse them with their own vessel type.
Master and all persons on board or ashore shall also comply with international, flag state and local laws and regulations.
Distribution of the manual on board shall be as per Chapter 3.1 of the Yellow Book.
Updated revision is available in the electronic application DocMap; DocMap contents are classified as controlled documentation.
Master may print copies as needed for operations; hard copies are classified as 'Uncontrolled Copies'.
If a hard copy is kept, the printed copy of a new version shall replace the old whenever the document is revised; reader is responsible for ensuring the paper copy is valid.
For inspection of the manual by external bodies, follow guidelines in SSMM Ch.11.3.
Manual approved by Vice President Global HSEQ and Systems; signed by Documentation Committee Chairman.

Ensure distribution on board per Yellow Book Ch.3.1
May print uncontrolled hard copies as needed and ensure they are the current version
All: All officers shall be familiar with and comply with applicable SSMM contents

chapters.title: General – 3.1 Definitions
chapters.purpose: Defines the terms used throughout the SSMM (accident, near accident, non-conformity, DPA, SMS, permit to work, critical operation, cyber incident, etc.) so that they are applied consistently on board and ashore.
key_requirements: Accident = an event with loss; Near Accident = an event without loss that could have caused harm/damage; Incident = accident, near accident or non-conformity.
Non-Conformity = non-fulfilment of a specified requirement (see Ch.9.1); Major NC = deviation posing serious threat to personnel, ship or environment requiring immediate corrective action.
Correction = 'quick fix' eliminating a specific incident; Corrective Action eliminates causes to prevent recurrence; Preventive Action eliminates causes of potential incidents.
Root Cause Analysis identifies causal factors, immediate causes and root causes and develops recommendations at each level.
DPA = person ashore with direct access to top management responsible to monitor safety/pollution prevention and ensure adequate shore support.
Company = organisation that has assumed ISM responsibility; for WSM it means the management centre responsible for full technical management.
Critical Operation = operation where an error may immediately cause an accident threatening lives, environment or ship; Special Operation = error becomes apparent only after hazard/accident.
Permit to Work = form signed by Authorised Person to Competent Person; a checklist identifying hazards, defining work scope, validity, time limits and exact location.
Coastal Waters = within 20 nm of coastline or 30 minutes sailing time from grounding line, whichever is lesser; Restricted Water = harbours, ports, pilotage or waters needing special caution.
Emergency Command Centre (ECC) = location predetermined by the Master from which emergency activities are coordinated.

Governing Documents = standing instructions all staff on board must comply with (see Ch.11.1); Record = document providing evidence of activities performed; Retention Period = period records are kept.
Intoxicating Substances = any substance affecting perceptive systems, e.g. alcohol, certain drugs (see Ch.6.3).
Cyber Incident = occurrence with actual/potential adverse consequences to onboard systems or data that may require response; Cyber Risk Management defined.
Bridge Officer = deck officer holding STCW D-certificate; Crew = all complement other than Master; Ship's staff = all including Master; Supernumeraries have no official role and no pay.
DOC issued to company and SMC issued to ship after successful external ISM audit; Internal SMS audits verify compliance with ISM Code.
Port State Control = process by which a nation exercises authority over foreign ships in its waters.

Master: Predetermines location of the Emergency Command Centre (ECC)
All: Apply SSMM definitions consistently; comply with Governing Documents as standing instructions

chapters.title: Shipboard Organization
chapters.purpose: Describes the Company organisation structure relevant to shipboard activity: vessel manager, Master's authority, the shipboard management team and the four shipboard departments.
key_requirements: 4.1.2 A dedicated vessel manager is responsible for operation of vessels under his charge and for coordination between ship and Company (role in Fig. 4.1.3).
4.1.2 Master has complete authority over all personnel on board, is responsible for implementing corporate policies and reports to the designated vessel manager (see Ch.5.1).
4.1.2 Shipboard management team = Master, Chief Engineer, Chief Officer and Second Engineer (First Engineer on some Norwegian ships), headed by the Master.
4.1.3 Shipboard organisation under the Master comprises four departments: Deck (Chief Officer), Engine (Chief Engineer), Catering (catering officer/chief steward) and Special Operations.
4.1.3 If only a Chief Cook is assigned, the Master assumes formal responsibility for the catering department.
4.1.3 Radio and communications functions come directly under the Master; on GMDSS vessels the Master is responsible for all communications.
4.1.3 Performance level of each function is a line management responsibility; Master is responsible for overall performance level on board.
4.1.3 Minimum manning is based on flag state requirements, trading area, special operational requirements, compliance with work and rest hour regulations and the Ship Security Plan.
4.1.3 On ISO 14001 / 50001 vessels all personnel shall be aware of environmental and energy efficiency aspects relevant to their role and act as departmental representative if required.
4.1.4 Special operations team leader (salvage, seismic etc.) is head of that department, responsible to the Master, and advises him on departmental, technical and administrative matters.
4.1.4 Special operations leader is responsible for safe management of the special operation, equipment handling and stowage; not a member of shipboard management but attends meetings as appropriate.

4.1.4 Special operations leader coordinates with Chief Officer and Chief Engineer for anti-pollution activity and is team leader for special operations emergencies (D24 General Emergency Instructions).
4.1.4 During a special operation there shall be direct communication and exchange of operational information between the special operations leader and the Master.

chapters.title: Master
chapters.purpose: Defines the Master's ultimate and overriding authority and his responsibilities for safety, security (incl. cyber), pollution prevention, documentation, training, drills, pre-departure/pre-arrival checks and reporting to the Company.
key_requirements: 5.1.1 Master has absolute and overriding authority and responsibility for decisions on safety, security (incl. cyber security) and pollution prevention; may request Company assistance. May appoint a Ship Cyber Security Officer.
5.1.2 Master shall report and record undesired events (incl. cyber incidents), unsafe practices and near accidents to the Company and rectify them if safely possible.
5.1.2 Master shall ensure watertight integrity at all times and review the watertight integrity checklist prior to sailing (Ch.7.4).
5.1.2 Master shall ensure ship's certificates are valid at all times and all books, drawings and documents are updated; relevant plans and certificates displayed as required.
5.1.2 Master shall verify joining crew hold appropriate certificates/documents required by flag state or international rules for the vessel type and trade.
5.1.2 Master is in charge of the radio station and its routines.
5.1.2 Master shall conduct Shipboard Management System Review (SMSR) covering safety, security, cyber, maintenance and environmental procedures during his tenure and report to Company per SSMM 12.2.
5.1.2 Master shall organise and preside over the safety committee (Ch.6.5).
5.1.2 Master shall conduct weekly inspection of the vessel with the HODs and enter findings in the deck logbook (or as per flag requirements).
5.1.2 Master shall implement the Drug and Alcohol Policy and manage onboard D&A tests (Ch.6.3).
5.1.2 If Master cannot retain command, the Chief Officer assumes temporary command; Master and Chief Officer shall not be absent from the vessel at the same time.
5.1.2 Master's order book (IMO recommendations, standing orders, daily instructions) shall be filled in every day at sea with time of entry and signature.

5.1.2 Official papers signed by Master bear the Company standard rubber stamp 'for WILHELMSEN SHIP MANAGEMENT ... for and on behalf of OWNERS as Agents only'; cargo papers (B/L) bear vessel stamp with name and GRT.
5.1.2 Master shall prepare ship-specific emergency preparedness plans (Ch.8.1), plan/execute/evaluate emergency drills and training with shipboard management and maintain records (Ch.8.2).
5.1.2 Master shall oversee training and familiarisation of crew, supernumeraries, riding squad, contractors and visitors; responsible for shipboard Docmap familiarisation.
5.1.2 Master shall use Form D-4 'Checklist by Change of Command' at handover; has authority to issue permits to work.

5.1.3 Pre-departure: navigation equipment and charts in order, B02 Preparation for Sea completed, adequate rested qualified crew, POB within SEC limit, familiarisation done, stowaway search, certificates valid, watertight integrity, stability and load line, UKC per BPM 4.3.3.2.6, cargo secured, machinery tested, LSA/FFA defect-free.
5.1.4 Pre-arrival: obtain all information for safe entry, complete B03 Preparation for Arrival Port, ensure equipment and procedures for safe entry in order; remedy malfunctions before entry.

5.1.5 Pre-arrival/pre-departure checks shall be recorded in the deck logbook; defects of important equipment reported to Company within 24 hours; deferred entry/departure ('Go/No-Go') reported to Company by quickest means.

Weekly vessel inspection with HODs recorded in deck log
Preside over safety committee; conduct SMSR; implement D&A policy

chapters.title: Chief Officer
chapters.purpose: Defines the authority, interrelation and responsibilities of the Chief Officer as head of the deck department, Master's deputy, Ship Security Officer, Safety Officer and person in charge of cargo, LSA, ballast water, garbage and deck records.
key_requirements: 5.2.1 C/O is officer-in-charge of the deck department, reports directly to the Master and takes over command if the Master is unable or absent.
5.2.1 C/O is an independent navigation watchkeeping officer and in charge of safe management of cargo operations and stowage (and ramps on car carriers).
5.2.1 C/O is Team 1 leader for fire-fighting (D24 General Emergency Instructions) and co-coordinator with C/E for anti-pollution activity.

5.2.1 C/O is the Ship Security Officer and the appointed Ship Safety Officer; Environmental Officer if trained per SSMM 6.1.9.6; Environmental and Energy Efficiency Officer on ISO 14001/50001 vessels.
5.2.1 C/O is in charge of the garbage management plan and records, ballast water management and records, and VOC emission records.
5.2.2 C/O shall plan and execute deck department operations, delegate jobs and regulate crew working hours to comply with regulations.
5.2.2 C/O shall report and record undesired events, unsafe practices and near accidents and rectify them if safely possible.
5.2.2 C/O shall ensure security duties are carried out per the Ship Security Plan.
5.2.2 C/O shall keep navigational watch at sea and usually be on the bridge during arrival/departure and mooring/unmooring.
5.2.2 C/O is responsible for maintenance of Life Saving Appliances and upkeep of the LSA Maintenance Record (BD13), assisted by C/E and designated crew.
5.2.2 C/O is responsible for maintenance and inventory control of oil pollution (SOPEP) equipment and assists C/E with FFA maintenance on request.

5.2.2 C/O maintains the deck logbook, Oil Record Book Part II (oil tankers), Cargo Record Book (chemical tankers), deck work-done records and the Cargo Handling and Lifting Equipment logbook / register of lifting equipment.
5.2.2 C/O supervises ballasting/deballasting in compliance with anti-pollution laws and ensures watertight integrity, stability and seaworthiness at all times, reporting to Master.
5.2.2 C/O supervises upkeep of hull, superstructure, deck fittings and accommodation spaces (not under C/E or catering) and prepares for deck department surveys.
5.2.2 C/O trains staff under his charge, monitors progress and addresses improvement areas with the Master (Ch.6.1); manages care, storage and testing of measuring instruments (Ch.10.5).
5.2.2 C/O prepares department-specific emergency plans approved by Master, assists Master with contingency plans per VCM, familiarises staff and conducts drills.
5.2.2 C/O supervises shipboard waste management and records (garbage management plan, Ch.7.18); provides inputs to the Shipboard Management System Review (Ch.12.2).
5.2.2 C/O has authority to issue permits to work and shall understudy the Master.

5.3.1 2/O reports to the Master for navigation matters and to the Chief Officer for safety, cargo and maintenance issues; co-coordinator with C/O for anti-pollution activity.
5.3.2 2/O shall understand and abide by relevant documentation and procedures and sign copies as instructed to indicate understanding.
5.3.2 2/O shall report undesired events, unsafe practices or near accidents to superior officers and rectify if safely possible.
5.3.2 2/O performs navigational watch at sea and supervises cargo work in port as assigned by Master or C/O.
5.3.2 2/O is responsible for voyage planning and maintenance/upkeep of ALL charts, publications, watchkeeping records, navigational warnings and weather reports.
5.3.2 2/O performs anchoring/berthing/mooring station duties and pre-pilotage/port checks on bridge equipment as instructed by the Master.
5.3.2 2/O performs security duties as required by the SSO and, on GMDSS vessels, radio duties as directed by the Master.
5.3.2 2/O assists in medical duties under Master/C/O supervision and in upkeep and inventory of the medical locker and equipment.
5.3.2 2/O assists in upkeep of LSA and FFA equipment as required by Master or C/O.
5.3.2 2/O is in charge of shipboard clocks and chronometers.
5.3.2 2/O prepares abstracts, forms and clerical duties delegated by the Master.
5.3.2 2/O participates actively in all drills and exercises and imparts training as instructed; member of safety committee if called upon.
5.3.2 2/O shall understudy the Chief Officer and maintain awareness of environmental and energy efficiency aspects (ISO accredited vessels).

chapters.title: Chief Engineer
chapters.purpose: Defines the authority, interrelation and responsibilities of the Chief Engineer as head of technical operations, fire-fighting supervisor, anti-pollution co-coordinator and person responsible for planned maintenance, FFA, bunkers and Oil Record Book Part I.
key_requirements: 5.6.1 C/E is in charge of technical operations, a member of shipboard management, responsible to and adviser of the Master on technical and administrative matters.
5.6.1 C/E is fire-fighting supervisor for the entire shipboard organisation with authority to train and plan fire drills; co-coordinator with C/O for anti-pollution activities.
5.6.2 C/E shall record and report undesired events, unsafe practices or near accidents to the Master and arrange rectification (Ch.9.1).
5.6.2 C/E plans and executes engine department operations, delegates jobs and regulates crew working hours to comply with regulations.
5.6.2 C/E ensures engine department security duties are carried out as required by the SSO.

5.6.2 C/E coordinates and is responsible for all repairs in all departments per the planned maintenance system, including regular testing/maintenance of safety and pollution equipment and systems not in regular use.
5.6.2 C/E is responsible for maintenance of Fire Fighting Appliances and upkeep of the FFA Maintenance Record (BE14), assisted by C/O and designated crew.
5.6.2 C/E provides technical assistance to C/O for LSA and oil pollution equipment maintenance on request.
5.6.2 C/E informs Master of bunker requirements and plans/supervises receipt, storage, transfer and consumption of fuel and lubes.
5.6.2 C/E ensures all local and international oil pollution laws are strictly observed and the Oil Record Book Part I is maintained as required by law.
5.6.2 C/E ensures manuals, records, books, forms and drawings under his charge are maintained, stored and updated.
5.6.2 C/E's order book (BE-13) shall be filled in every day with time and signature; entries read and initialled by each engineer on joining and before taking over watch.
5.6.2 Routine orders must be prepared for key procedures on systems/equipment whose failure could endanger safety and environment; understanding and compliance ensured.
5.6.2 C/E assists Master with ship-specific emergency plans (VCM appendix), prepares department-specific emergency plans approved by Master, familiarises staff and conducts drills.

chapters.title: Personal Protection Equipment
chapters.purpose: Establishes the Company minimum standard for personal protective equipment (PPE) used by ship's personnel, ensuring all onboard know the importance and proper use of PPE to improve safety at work and reduce personal injury.
key_requirements: 6.2.2 Guidelines are the Company's minimum standard; flag state requirements in excess of the minimum shall apply.
6.2.2 Jewellery such as chains, bracelets and rings that may pose an additional hazard shall not be worn during work.
6.2.2 Additional PPE requirements may be proposed by the safety committee and forwarded to the Company.
6.2.2 All PPE requested and used onboard must be of the approved type (lifejackets/PFDs: Wheel Mark or equivalent).
6.2.2 HODs are responsible for requesting, storage and upkeep of safety equipment; safety officer and safety representative(s) monitor its use.
6.2.2 PPE must be worn as per the WSM PPE matrix (Ch.6.2.3) and selected according to the hazard and the findings of the risk assessment / toolbox talk.
6.2.2 All PPE shall be received by crew before they undertake their first task onboard.
6.2.2 Training is to be given on donning and use of PPE, particularly complex equipment such as safety harnesses.
6.2.2 PPE must be issued in correct size/shape to fit the user, worn correctly and replaced as needed.
6.2.2 Visitors shall be provided with appropriate PPE; contractors working onboard shall wear PPE per the WSM PPE matrix.
6.2.2 Synthetic material shall be avoided for tasks involving flames or heat (refer Ch.7.1.4 for hot work protection).
6.2.2 Further PPE details are in the Personal Handbook available in each cabin.
6.2.3 Respirators give no protection in oxygen-deficient atmospheres and shall never be used in enclosed spaces; only SCBA protects in such conditions.
6.2.3 Canister respirators have a shelf life and renewal criteria; correct cartridge/canister function must be chosen for the dust, fumes or gases present.
6.2.3 Safety harness with lifeline is required whenever working at height; inflatable working lifevest/PFD when working overside or where risk of falling in water exists (Ch.7.1.5).
6.2.3 Insulated rubber gloves, boots and mat with rated voltage are required for electrical work (Ch.7.1.11).
6.2.3 Cut-resistant gloves are to be used in the galley for knife work; cooks apron, clothing and hat to maintain food hygiene.
6.2.3 Safety helmet, safety shoes and boiler suit / high-visibility clothing are location-based PPE for deck, engine room, cargo decks and mooring/anchoring operations.

chapters.title: Drug And Alcohol Guidelines
chapters.purpose: Ensures adherence to the corporate drug and alcohol policy, safeguards ship staff from drug and alcohol abuse, and sets rules for consumption, purchase, sale and testing of alcohol and handling of drugs onboard (ref. OCIMF guidelines).
key_requirements: 6.3.2 The Master is responsible for onboard compliance with the corporate drug and alcohol policy.
6.3.4 Illegitimate drugs are completely banned; alcoholic beverages above 22% alcohol are not permitted and no alcohol may be brought onboard privately.
6.3.4 No alcohol (incl. beer) during working hours/overtime and for 4 hours prior to work or watch; BAC must be 0% when starting work/watch and max 0.04% off duty.
6.3.4 ZERO alcohol policy applies to offshore vessels, DWM vessels, GPO Heavylift vessels and Frontline vessels managed by WSM; Customer D&A policies apply where applicable.
6.3.4 No alcohol shall be served to a pilot before or while performing duties; Master shall implement port state restrictions.
6.3.4 Crew may not possess more than 1L alcohol, 200 cigarettes or 24 cans of beer at any time; everyone must report violations to ship's management immediately.
6.3.5/6.3.6 Alcohol purchase is on behalf of the Company; no personal income from sale; sale only with Master's approval, not during working hours, not to persons under 18, not traded.
6.3.6 Recommended maximum allowance: 0.7 L beer/cider per crew per day OR 2 L wine per crew per month, or proportionate mix.
6.3.7.2 At least once a year an Authorised Service Provider conducts unannounced D&A tests on tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and offshore vessels.

6.3.7.3 Onboard 'No Notice' alcometer random tests on tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and Frontline vessels at intervals not exceeding 1 month; Master tests crew, C/E and C/O together test the Master.

6.3.7.3 Results recorded against each member on a crew list sheet; Company initiates unannounced tests by phone/e-mail at least twice a year (quarterly for tankers/gas carriers, results within 2 hours).
6.3.7.4 Post accident/incident alcohol test for involved personnel on all vessels, recorded in the ship's logbook.
6.3.7.4 US waters Serious Marine Incident (46 CFR 16): alcohol test within 2 hours, urine drug sample within 32 hours to accredited lab, USCG form completed and sent via agent.
6.3.7.5 Master may test any staff suspected of intoxication (especially watchkeepers) with the alcometer and record results.
6.3.8 All drug and alcohol tests conducted shall be recorded in the deck logbook; exceeding limits leads to disciplinary action (6.3.9).
6.3.10 Charterer minimum requirements: notices on drug dangers, D&A policy posted conspicuously, test equipment available, record of tests (date and persons tested).
6.3.11 Staff showing signs of drug use shall be taken off duty and tested by a competent person at first opportunity.

6.3.12 Drugs found onboard: inform Company, do not touch without PPE, witness by another officer, photograph, log full details, post guard, full signed report; nobody leaves until interviewed by authorities.

chapters.title: Communication
chapters.purpose: Defines channels and control of communication amongst ship staff, between ship and Company and with external parties, including closed-loop communication, position/daily/weekly reporting, Company response to failure to report, accident reporting and GDPR data protection.
key_requirements: 6.4.2 Confidential matters designated by the Master or Company shall not be disclosed to unauthorised persons.
6.4.3 Working and command language is English and shall be logged in the ship's logbook; instructions must be clear and to the point.
6.4.3 Closed-loop communication: recipient repeats the order, verbally confirms understanding, follow-up check where necessary.
6.4.3 On joining, all staff familiarise with communication means/equipment applicable to their duties, especially emergency communication; exercises and training conducted.
6.4.3 In emergency follow VCM communication procedures and muster list; administrative/disciplinary matters go via department head, then Master with HOD present.
6.4.4 Master controls and despatches all ship-Company correspondence (may delegate); all correspondence sent with Master's consent; official documents addressed to the Company not individuals.
6.4.4 Master shall immediately report events with serious safety or commercial consequences (cargo stoppages, berth incidents, deviations, medical emergencies).
6.4.4 Verbal report at first opportunity, phone discussions followed up by e-mail.
6.4.4 C/O and C/E with e-mail may communicate directly with the office keeping the Master in copy; signature rubber stamps prohibited except on official documents.
6.4.5 Master is responsible for position reporting; failure to send timely reports is treated as a serious procedural lapse (Company response per 6.4.9).
6.4.5.4 Departure report: name/call sign, place/date/time, ROB bunkers and FW, visual drafts F/A/Mid, ETA next port.
6.4.5.4 Daily position report (SOLAS V/28.2) around 1200LT on international voyages over 48 h via form DE65: position, course/speed, external and internal conditions affecting safe operation.

chapters.title: Work And Rest Hours
chapters.purpose: Ensures ship's staff are rested and fit for duty by planning work/rest hours, posting the shipboard working arrangements table (DE47b), keeping rest hour records (DE47) within STCW/MLC limits, and reporting anticipated or actual breaches to the Company.
key_requirements: 6.6.2 Work and rest hours and duty rotation shall be planned in advance, especially before port arrival when workload is heavy.

6.6.2 Master shall post a table of shipboard working arrangements for every position (DE47b) in an accessible location, in the working language and English, showing scheduled daily work hours at sea and in port.
6.6.3 Maximum hours of work: 14 h in any 24 h and 72 h in any 7 days; or minimum rest: 10 h in any 24 h and 77 h in any 7 days.
6.6.3 Rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one at least 6 h; interval between consecutive rest periods not to exceed 14 h.
6.6.3 STCW 2010 exceptions only where flag state / collective agreement allow: weekly rest not less than 70 h, exception not more than two consecutive weeks.

6.6.3 Interval between exceptions at least twice the exception duration; under exception daily rest may be split into three periods (one at least 6 h, others at least 1 h), not exceeding two 24-h periods in any 7 days.
6.6.3 Daily rest hour records (DE47) shall be properly recorded and authenticated by the Master or designated officer; verification done during weekly PMC meetings; seafarer receives a copy.
6.6.3 Electronic rest hour systems may be used if allowed by flag state and its guidelines followed.
6.6.3 Rest requirements may be suspended in emergencies or overriding operational conditions; adequate rest given afterwards.
6.6.3 Musters and drills shall be conducted to minimise disturbance of rest periods and not induce fatigue.
6.6.3 Seafarers on call (e.g. UMS) shall receive compensatory rest as soon as practicable if rest is disturbed by call-outs; any violation of rest hours must be recorded.
6.6.3 Master may require work necessary for immediate safety of ship, persons, cargo or assistance to others in distress and suspend the schedule until normal situation restored.
6.6.4 Master informs Company as soon as practicable with a proposal (stoppage, additional manpower) when a breach is anticipated, when a breach occurs, or when exceptions are needed.
6.6.4 Master takes corrective action and reports trends or consistent breaches in certain areas or port rotations to the Company.

chapters.title: Health Onboard

6.8.5.2 Cabins well maintained; A/C filters and ducts inspected and cleaned per a maintenance plan; condensation trays self-draining and disinfected.
6.8.5.2 Toilets and drains kept hygienic, broken flushes repaired without delay.
6.8.5.2 Cleaning gear stored in designated lockers away from food areas; ship's hospital kept clean; medicine lockers maintained and expired medicines replenished.

6.8.5.2 NIS vessels: all-out cleaning of galley and accommodation at least 3 times/year.
6.8.5.4 Food handled, prepared and stored hygienically; garbage areas segregated from food areas; cold room temperatures per manufacturer; balanced diet respecting religious/cultural needs.
6.8.5.4 Portion management to avoid leftovers.

6.8.5.4 Potable water tanks labelled with capacity; potable water risk assessment (DE54) with control points; tanks included in PMS; drinking water tested every 6 months (samples ashore) or when quality unsatisfactory.

6.8.5.5 Vector Management Plan vessel specific where required.

6.8.5.7 Health hazards ashore at port calls made known to all onboard with preventive measures taken with health authorities / company doctor.
6.8.5.8 Health literature and posters available in common rooms; healthy lifestyle discussed at safety meetings and recorded in DE50 section 12.

6.8.6 Designated smoking areas marked with signs.
6.8.7 Provisions quality inspected; deteriorated/expired food rejected and value noted in Portage Bill; monthly inventory control and reporting; 'used by'/expired products never served.

6.8.7.2 Master and Chief Cook ensure storage routines: receiving checklist (expiry/min shelf life, frozen at -18°C or less, fresh quality, insects/cockroaches, packaging), FIFO rotation, storerooms sectioned.
6.8.7.2 No overstocking.
6.8.8 Health records kept and sent to Company as relevant.

chapters.title: Permit To Work
chapters.purpose: Establishes the Permit To Work (PTW) system (critical operation) so that all risk elements are considered in the planning, approval, preparation, execution and completion of work, defining roles, permit validity, forms (PTW-100 certificate, PTW-101 isolation certificate, PTW-01 to PTW-13 checklists) and records.

7.1.J Issuing Authority issues permits only to trained competent persons, coordinates simultaneous operations, ensures risk assessments.
7.1.J Site examination and correct completion/signing of permits and isolation certificates.

7.1.J Permit Holder prepares the PTW, ensures precautions are met, examines site on suspension/restart and completion, signs out and returns the permit; Permit Holder and Issuing Authority cannot be the same person.

7.1.J Area Authority (HOD unless otherwise nominated) inspects the work area, verifies readiness, may refuse/withdraw/close a PTW and ensures close-out; Area Authority and Isolation Responsible cannot be the same person.
7.1.J Isolation Responsible (qualified equipment operator, e.g. engineer/electrician) carries out and reinstates isolations and issues Isolation Certificate PTW-101 per lockout/tagout.
7.1.J Permit Controller (Safety Officer or OOW) identifies permit tasks/locations, cross-references interacting permits and ensures permits are closed within duration.

7.1.K All individuals incl. contractors understand the PTW system, do not start permit work until authorised, and strictly adhere to permit conditions.
7.1.K Master seeks shore PTW from port authority for hot work alongside via agent.
7.1.L An approved PTW must not be changed; changes require reprocessing (except added operational/safety preparations).
7.1.M PTW valid maximum 12 hours, not transferable between shifts/personnel; may be extended max 4 hours with same crew within work/rest hour limits; PTWs reviewed in daily meetings.
7.1.M Work stopped and site secured on emergency alarm, unfulfilled preconditions or dangerous situation; restart only with Issuing Authority approval.

7.1.N PTW-100 copies: original displayed at permit control location (e.g. bridge), 1st copy with Permit Holder at worksite, 2nd copy with Area Authority; RA copy in RA library; Toolbox Talk recorded per SSMM 9.3.
7.1.N Completed PTWs filed numerically from 001/year with isolation certificates and checklists, retained per Yellow Book.
7.1.N PTW log maintained at permit control location (number, location, type, issue and closing date/time).

chapters.title: Lockout and Tagout
chapters.purpose: Critical operation procedure to protect personnel from inadvertent energisation of machinery or systems by requiring lockout/tagout and an Isolation Certificate (PTW-101) under the PTW system for electrical, mechanical and long-term isolations.
key_requirements: 7.1.1.D Forms: PTW-100 Permit to Work Certificate, PTW-101 Isolation Certificate, DE54 Risk Assessment – Lockout Tagout.
7.1.1.E LOTO required for all tasks with risk of accidental turn-on: electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic systems, fuel engines, working aloft, enclosed spaces, opening manholes of ballast/FW tanks.
7.1.1.E Vessel shall have a lockout/tagout kit with appropriate tags and lockout devices suitable for onboard equipment.
7.1.1.E LOTO devices used are noted in Isolation Certificate PTW-101 and the certificate number entered on PTW-100.
7.1.1.E Permit Holder identifies all parts/switches/valves to be shut down, all energy sources (hydraulic, pneumatic, springs, gravity, electric), advises everyone affected, and keeps the lock keys.
7.1.1.E Energy sources isolated, movable parts blocked, spring energy released, hydraulic/pneumatic bled down, suspended parts lowered before work.
7.1.1.E Tags show out-of-order status, reason, name, date and time; tagging by Isolation Responsible and removed only after locks removed, system tested and restart approved.
7.1.1.E Only Permit Holder can authorise lock removal/power on.
7.1.1.F An Isolation Certificate is required before work starts confirming safety from liquid, air/gas pressure, mechanical, electrical and fuel hazards.

7.1.1.G Type and method of isolation decided by Area Authority and Isolation Responsible with reference to electrical/piping drawings; padlocks used to lock off isolated equipment, keys deposited in a safe location.
7.1.1.G All isolations recorded in the Isolation Certificate and clearly labelled at the point of isolation.
7.1.1.H Electrical isolations: removed fuses kept away from work area, removed plugs barriered, breakers locked off with padlock; only competent persons approved by Area Authority.
7.1.1.H Isolation checked ('check for dead') with rated test equipment.
7.1.1.H/J If isolation spans shifts, the oncoming Area Authority must reconfirm isolation status before work recommences.
7.1.1.J Mechanical isolation hierarchy: physical disconnection, spades/line blinds, double block and bleed, closed and locked valves; two valves in line preferred; leak test after isolation.
7.1.1.K Personal isolations are prohibited.
7.1.1.L Long term isolations detailed in PTW-101; maximum 4 weeks, re-authorised by Area Authority at least every 7 days; new certificate beyond 4 weeks; PTW required for reinstatement work.
7.1.1.L Issuing Authority holds all long-term isolation certificates with a copy kept by the Permit Controller.
7.1.1.M Isolation requested from Area Authority, who consults affected departments and nominates a competent person to perform the isolation and complete the certificate.

Ensures LOTO kit available onboard

chapters.title: Enclosed Spaces
chapters.purpose: Critical operation procedure defining enclosed spaces, requiring their identification and marking, and setting the permit, atmosphere testing, ventilation, watch, rescue and post-work requirements to prevent accidents when entering or working in such spaces.
key_requirements: 7.1.2.D PTW-100, PTW-02 Safety Checklist for enclosed space entry, PTW-01 Gas Measurement Records, PTW-101 Isolation Certificate, DE54 risk assessments (enclosed spaces / identification), DE52 water tightness check.
7.1.2.D DE28 tank cleaning checklist (tankers).
7.1.2.E Shipboard management carries out a risk assessment to identify all enclosed spaces; a ship-specific list (name, location, number of entrances, remarks) is maintained onboard.
7.1.2.E All enclosed space entrances marked in contrasting colour 'DANGER ENCLOSED SPACE – STRICTLY NO UNAUTHORISED ENTRY' (or per flag); central warning signs where entrances cannot be marked.
7.1.2.F Access physically restricted until the space is certified gas free; no entry unless atmosphere tested at 20.8-21% oxygen and free from toxic gases; no entry without an authorised valid PTW.
7.1.2.G Master ensures implementation of procedures, compliance with flag/company/port rules, authorises the permit.
7.1.2.G Suspends it on breach (e.g. ventilation stops) and familiarises crew through regular enclosed space entry and rescue drills.

7.1.2.G Permit Holder carries out risk assessment, determines space is safe, completes the entry permit jointly with Isolation Responsible, Gas Tester, Area Authority and team leader (separate permit per space).

7.1.2.G Ensures frequent gas testing and continuous ventilation; watchman documents persons entering/leaving, maintains radio contact at agreed intervals with persons inside, Permit Holder and Permit Controller.
7.1.2.G Alerts on changed conditions and keeps rescue equipment ready at the entrance.
7.1.2.H Only jobs essential to safe operation are done in enclosed spaces; Master evaluates the need with the Planned Maintenance Committee.
7.1.2.K Officers must understand gas measuring equipment limitations; equipment calibrated per Ch.10.5; sensors stored in silica receptacle with tag and date-in-use marked.
7.1.2.K Duplicate personal gas detectors recommended on tankers.
7.1.2.K Gas readings on PTW-01 taken from outside at top, middle and bottom through as many openings as possible incl. dead spots; ventilation stopped about 10 minutes before pre-entry tests.
7.1.2.K Entry criteria: oxygen 20.8-21%, flammable vapour below 1% LFL, no toxic gases; max 30 minutes between test and entry and between tests while occupied; frequency recorded on PTW-01.
7.1.2.L Ventilation before entry and continuous effective ventilation throughout the operation; new permit if ventilation interrupted more than 1 hour (Ch.7.1).
7.1.2.M Before removing covers check for pressure/temperature differences; guard openings with railing/barrier; all energy sources isolated, locked out and tagged on PTW-101 with keys held safely.

chapters.title: Cold Work
chapters.purpose: Critical operation procedure establishing controlled permit-to-work procedures for cold work (non-ignition work such as grit blasting, power tools, chipping) especially in gas hazardous areas and on pressurised systems.
key_requirements: 7.1.3.C Cold work includes grit blasting, mechanically powered tools, pneumatic grinders, chipping hammers and scrapers that may cause incendive sparks.
7.1.3.C In gas hazardous areas it requires risk assessment and mitigation before starting.
7.1.3.C Gas hazardous areas: tankers – cargo tank deck area, within 500 mm of bunker tanks/oil pipework and 20 m of ventilators.
7.1.3.C Non-tankers – within 20 m of ventilators or open hatches with gas-evolving cargoes and 500 mm of bunker tanks/oil pipework.
7.1.3.D Forms: DE54 Risk Assessment – Cold Work and – Pressurised Systems, PTW-03 Safety Checklist for Cold Work, PTW-100 Permit to Work Certificate, PTW-101 Isolation Certificate.

7.1.3.E No work may commence until the permit has been issued; PTW-100 accompanied by supporting documents (vessel manager's concurrence where required, applicable checklists, gas measurement records).

7.1.3.E If conditions change, Permit Holder or any crew member shall STOP work and inform the Issuing Authority/Permit Controller to cancel the permit; resume only with a new permit after conditions normalise.
7.1.3.F Only the Master is authorised to approve cold work in a gas hazardous or dangerous area.
7.1.3.F Area Authority ensures staff involved are competent, experienced and understand requirements, procedures, tools and hazards.
7.1.3.F Permit Holder monitors that work proceeds as per toolbox talk and safety conditions are maintained; each worker responsible for own safety and PPE.
7.1.3.G Permit Holder completes risk assessment and toolbox talk identifying simultaneous conflicting operations, vapour/pressure release, impact, noise and weather hazards.
7.1.3.G Risk reduction measures and an agreed work plan (PPE, back-up, compressed air, fire pump, cranes, timing).
7.1.3.H Cold work in gas hazardous/dangerous area requires PTW-100, PTW-02 enclosed space checklist and PTW-03 cold work checklist all completed and satisfied.
7.1.3.I Cold work on pressurised systems requires PTW-100, PTW-03 and Isolation Certificate PTW-101 completed and satisfied.
7.1.3.J Post-work inspection: safe completion and securing of equipment, tools and PPE cleaned and stowed, housekeeping of work area.

chapters.title: Hot Work
chapters.purpose: Critical operation procedure establishing controlled permit-to-work procedures for hot work (welding, cutting, heating, soldering and non-intrinsically-safe equipment in gas hazardous areas), including restrictions, office concurrence, roles, fire precautions, enclosed space/aloft/pipeline hot work and protective equipment.
key_requirements: 7.1.4.D Forms: DE54 Risk Assessment – Hot Work, PTW-01 Gas Measurement Record, PTW-04 Safety Checklist for Hot Work, PTW-100 Permit to Work Certificate, PTW-101 Isolation Certificate.
7.1.4.E Only one hot work operation at a time; multiple locations only after assessing available resources before issuing permits.

7.1.4.E Tankers: hot work prohibited during bunkering, cargo operations, COW, tank cleaning or whenever cargo tank vapours are released; non-tankers: hot work outside a designated space prohibited during bunkering.
7.1.4.G No hot work may commence before the permit is issued; PTW-100 accompanied by supporting documents (Vessel Manager concurrence, checklists, gas measurement records).

7.1.4.J On non-tankers Vessel Manager concurrence for hot work in gas hazardous areas, fuel tanks, associated piping and gas hazardous machinery spaces.
7.1.4.J Master's written request must include description, reason, vessel location, start/end date-time, preparations and safety precautions, with a copy of the risk assessment attached.
7.1.4.K Master/Issuing Authority decides if hot work is justified and safe (supported by RA), issues permit just prior to work, monitors controls.
7.1.4.K Cancels on breach and ensures atmosphere tests of work and adjacent areas are recorded.

7.1.4.K Area Authority and Permit Holder inspect work area, adjacent areas and equipment, maintain distances from bunker tanks/pipelines, jointly complete the permit and ensure continuous ventilation.
7.1.4.K Responsible Officer (may be Safety Representative, not involved in the work) monitors compliance, regular atmosphere tests incl. after breaks, informs Master to retract permit on breach.
7.1.4.K Ensures monitoring at least 30 minutes after completion.
7.1.4.K Fire watchman keeps continual fire watch until completion and 30 minutes after, never leaves post unless relieved, communicates with Permit Holder and workers.
7.1.4.K Never use oxygen from cylinders to blow dust off the body – fatal accidents have occurred.

7.1.4.L RA and toolbox talk, area isolated and cleaned of flammables (incl. reverse side of bulkheads), adjacent spaces checked/gas freed, continuous ventilation, atmosphere tests (PTW-01) throughout.
7.1.4.L At least 500 mm from fuel tank bulkheads/piping.

7.1.4.L Fire precautions: minimum two extinguishers (one for minor work), at least one pressurised fire hose per area at risk, means to smother sparks/slag; equipment not removed from Fire Control Plan locations.
7.1.4.L Controlled access continued until no fire risk.
7.1.4.M Tankers comply strictly with ISGOTT Rev.6 Ch.9.4.5; non-tankers normally no hot work in gas hazardous areas – emergency only with special RA and Company concurrence.
7.1.4.M Within 500 m of an offshore installation OIM permission and installation PTW apply.
7.1.4.N Hot work in enclosed spaces under Ch.7.1.2 control; oil pipelines through the space flushed with water; heating coils blown through and opened.
7.1.4.N Spaces adjacent to fuel/cargo tanks treated as gas hazardous – all spaces within 30 m gas freed, inerted to 2% HC, or water filled.
7.1.4.O Hot work on pipelines in situ only if item cannot be removed to designated space; disconnect by cold work, blank pipe ends, clean and gas free, ventilate and monitor exhaust for HC vapour.
7.1.4.P Hot work aloft/overside under Ch.7.1.5; flammable material below removed/protected from falling sparks considering wind; hull hot work within cargo tank area treated as gas hazardous.
7.1.4.Q Post hot work: monitor area at least 30 minutes or until no fire risk; restore disturbed items; clean and stow tools and PPE.
7.1.4.S Electric welding equipment inspected before each use, earthed; supply connections in gas free space, cables in good condition routed over gas free/inerted spaces.
7.1.4.S Earth return cable direct to machine – ship's structure not used as earth return.
7.1.4.S PPE for hot work: welding mask/eye protection with correct filter shade (gas: shade 3-7 by acetylene flow.
7.1.4.S Arc: shade 7-14 by amperage), leather gloves, leather apron, long-sleeved natural fibre overalls, ear protection; clothing dry and free of oil/grease.

chapters.title: Working Aloft And Overside
chapters.purpose: Critical operation procedure for the safe execution of work aloft and overside (any location with a risk of falling to a lower level), covering planning, hazard identification, hierarchy of controls, fall protection equipment, ladders, work baskets, rail trolleys, scaffolding, inspection intervals and emergency rescue.
key_requirements: 7.1.5.E Forms: PTW-100 Permit to Work Certificate, PTW-05 Safety Checklist for working aloft/overside, DE54 Risk Assessment; ref. DE56 Authorisation to Operate Lifting Appliances.
7.1.5.G All work aloft/overside planned and risk assessed; simple tasks may need only a toolbox talk, complex work a formal RA, and depending on severity a permit to work.
7.1.5.H RA considers whether work at height can be avoided, fall distance, access, equipment, rescue method, need for isolation permit (PTW-101) and nearby operations.

7.1.5.I Hierarchy of controls: avoid work at height, prevent falls, minimise consequences; crew working overside must wear inflatable lifevest and safety harness with adequate safety line, connected to an anchor point.

7.1.5.I Inertia reels attached directly to the harness D-ring, no lanyard used with them, not used as working support, sited vertical to 30 degrees, never over an edge; consult manufacturer for persons above 100 kg.
7.1.5.I Equipment checked before use and fall-arrest rated; shackles not used for securing equipment or carrying people; certified anchor point used; connect new anchor before releasing old.
7.1.5.I Do not climb above anchor point; tools carried in a secure tool belt/pouch; area below cordoned off against falling objects considering wind, deflection and bounce.
7.1.5.J Connectors (karabiners/snap hooks) must be self-closing and double-action locking; steel preferred; avoid side-loading.
7.1.5.K Anchor points must be structurally sound; a single person anchor point shall support 15 kN; anchor straps inspected and kept off sharp/hot edges.
7.1.5.M Helmets must be fitted with a chin strap and it must be used when working at height.

7.1.5.N Ladders marked with a unique number, inspected before use, designed to a recognised standard; one person at a time; non-conductive ladders near electrical circuits; face ladder, no tools in hands.

7.1.5.N Portable ladders (steps/trestle) not used where fall risk exceeds 2 m; extension ladders at 1:4 ratio, extending at least 900 mm beyond platform, secured or footed; used for access not as a working platform.
7.1.5.O Suspended work baskets must be approved type (not home-made), workers secured to anchor point before lifting; baskets are lifting equipment inspected/certified every 6 months.
7.1.5.O PTW and RA before use (landing areas, crane driver communication and line of sight).

7.1.5.P Manned rail trolleys/baskets not used while vessel underway; locking devices disengaged only when repositioning; inspected/certified every 12 months (or per flag/maker); PTW and RA including rescue.
7.1.5.P Maker's maintenance info kept onboard.

7.1.5.Q Scaffolding erected/dismantled by competent persons under competent supervision; PTW and documented task-specific RA; certified material inspected; erected in port (at sea only after thorough RA).
7.1.5.Q Scaffold above 5 m requires personnel with an approved scaffolding course; below 5 m instruction by manager in charge documented; harness with fall arrester used when erecting.

7.1.5.R Inspection by competent person recorded in PMS: fixed anchorage points, fixed fall protection, work baskets/rail trolleys every 12 months; portable harnesses, lanyards, slings, rescue equipment every 3 months.
7.1.5.R Defective equipment removed, tagged or destroyed immediately.
7.1.5.S Rescue procedure developed before using fall arrest equipment: unconscious person rescued within 5 minutes (suspension trauma), rescue equipment at site, no lone working, communications.
7.1.5.S Rescue boat and crew ready, lifebuoy with line at work site.

chapters.title: Lifting Operations
chapters.purpose: Critical operation procedure ensuring vessels have routines for all lifting operations (to/from and internal, ship-to-ship, subsea) conducted safely under flag/charterer regulations (ILO 152, LOLER, NORSOK, IMCA), covering records, roles, lift categorisation, planning, pre-use checks, stability, lifting persons, communications and stop-work authority.
key_requirements: 7.1.7.E Forms: PTW-100, PTW-07 Safety checklist for lifting/crane operations, DE54 Risk Assessment, DE56 Authorisation to Operate Lifting Appliances, DE76 Lift Plan, PM13 Lifting Equipment Log.

7.1.7.F A Lifting Equipment Register (form prescribed by flag/class) is maintained for all cargo-handling lifting appliances and loose gear; other lifting gear (slings, strops, chain blocks) recorded in PM13 or PMS.

7.1.7.F Original records kept securely in a central location, available to inspectors on request; PMS jobs established to review documentation at examination intervals; records retained per regulatory requirements.
7.1.7.G Competent person (typically Master, C/O, C/E or experienced officer) plans and supervises lifts; lift supervisor (officer or Bosun) supervises lift and team.
7.1.7.G Heavy lift = non-routine lift exceeding 80% of crane SWL.
7.1.7.H Master has ultimate responsibility that crew are trained and aware of duties and must verify all lifts and lift plans, including project/engineered lifts by operators, approving every lift.
7.1.7.H Lifting team minimum: lift supervisor, load handler (banksman/slinger/signalman/rigger) and lifting equipment operator, who must have certification, training and competence.

7.1.7.I Bridge must be informed before any lift; vessel movement, stability, weather, crane limitations/modes, SIMOPS and adjacent structures considered; emergency modes never used to exceed capacities.
7.1.7.I All personnel operating cranes and lifting equipment must be approved by the Master (DE56).
7.1.7.J All cranes and lifting equipment certified, annually colour coded (UK flag) or otherwise identified, marked, in good condition and used per manufacturer's instructions.
7.1.7.K All lifts require a lift plan; routine lifts (gangway, provisions, garbage skip) use a generic lift plan/RA reviewed in a toolbox talk; if in doubt categorise as non-routine.
7.1.7.K Non-routine and heavy lifts require a permit to work (PTW-100) and completed PTW-07 checklist.

7.1.7.M Lift plan prepared by a competent person based on RA, defining resources, responsibilities, equipment, pre-use checks, communication methods and language; pre-lift meeting before non-routine lifts.
7.1.7.M MOC if procedures change; clear pick-up and lay-down areas within crane radius; cargo and containers secured against shifting; wheeled equipment directly restrained.

7.1.7.N Pre-use checks at least once each working day/shift: operator holds DE56, visual check, function test per manufacturer, emergency stop test, defects reported; equipment not used if safety features fail.
7.1.7.O Lift plans must consider effects on vessel trim, heel and stability, especially heavy lifts and transfers to other floating units.
7.1.7.P Lifting of persons eliminated where possible; otherwise only with equipment specifically designed/adapted and marked 'suitable for lifting persons' where required by regulators.

7.1.7.Q Common language or established signal system displayed for the lift team; designated signallers identifiable by reflective jackets; lift area kept clear of uninvolved persons; stop if any signal unclear.
7.1.7.R Any person may stop the lifting operation on a potential safety issue (unclear signal, alarm, competence exceeded, communication failure).

7.1.7.T LOLER (UK waters): lifting equipment strong, stable, suitable, marked with SWL (accessories too), thoroughly examined before first use and at least 12-monthly by a competent person with report kept.
7.1.7.T All personnel using lifting equipment shall receive adequate training, instruction and information on the equipment provided.

7.2.4.1 Watch levels and additional watch requirements set at Master's discretion within BPM 2.4 limits; OOW role per BPM Ch.3 Sec.2; with pilot onboard BPM 3.2.4.16 applies.

7.2.4.2 Engine room adequately manned during transit within SSMM 7.15 limits; Chief Engineer briefs duty engine staff on transit details.

chapters.purpose: Special operation guidelines for precautions when heavy weather is forecast, to minimise personal injury, pollution, structural/machinery damage, loss of watertight integrity or manoeuvrability and cargo damage, at sea and while moored or anchored (B10 checklist, DE54 risk assessments).

7.3.6 When heavy weather expected or encountered (SOLAS V/31).

7.3.7 Master with HODs conducts a ship- and voyage-specific risk assessment (hull, manoeuvrability, machinery, crew/passengers) identifying movables to secure; contingency plans for course change or shelter.
7.3.7 Check stability, watertight integrity and equipment condition; reduce speed and adjust course to reduce wave impact; re-assess work RAs during heavy weather considering fatigue.

7.3.7 Rig safety lines/hand ropes; crew working on exposed decks wear lifejackets/lifelines, bridge informed of identity and location and monitors them until back in shelter; regular drills and briefings.
7.3.7 HODs check their areas periodically during and immediately after heavy weather and report damage/risks to the Master.
7.3.8 Master completes B10 checklist with actions confirmed by HODs when heavy weather forecast; refer MSC.1/Circ.1228 on synchronous/parametric rolling and surf-riding.

7.3.8.1 Deck: bridge manned per BPM 2.4; avoid jobs in exposed areas; secure all deck movables away from vents; periodic watch on deck objects; recheck cargo and LSA lashings before/during/after; lock cranes.

7.3.8.1 Keep scuppers clear; close all deck openings, watertight doors, deadlights, storm covers and portholes; extra anchor lashings; additional steering motors; adjust tank levels for stability/trim.
7.3.8.1 Heavy weather ballast taken as decided by Master within loading manual stresses and stability booklet; alter course to minimise sloshing while filling (SSMM 7.12.7).
7.3.8.1 Monitor RPM, speed, list, roll angle and report significant changes.

7.3.8.2 Engine: engine room manned per SSMM 7.15; observe machinery operating limits; transfer bilges to holding tank and avoid pumping out; refill sumps without overfilling; secure spares and lock overhead cranes.
7.3.8.2 Drain water from fuel tanks frequently; additional generators running/stand-by; monitor FO/LO filters; frequent rounds; inform bridge of overloading; keep floors oil-free and plates secured.
7.3.8.2 Skylight and funnel doors shut; check steering gear regularly.
7.3.8.3 Catering/accommodation: secure crockery, open containers, bond and provision stores; galley staff regular inspection rounds reporting abnormalities to HOD; secure movables in common areas.
7.3.8.3 Consider closing high-risk venues.
7.3.9 Shelter in port does not remove all risk; assess whether to stay alongside, shift berth/anchorage or go to sea; liaise with agent and port authorities.
7.3.9.1 Moored: local weather updates, additional generators and engines on stand-by, adequate bridge/ER manning for emergency departure, shore mooring team, pilot and tug availability verified.
7.3.9.1 Consider suspending cargo ops and shore leave, secure gangway, extra mooring lines, frequent mooring rounds.

7.3.9.2 Anchored: consider critical wind velocity and proximity of other vessels, recheck swinging circle when paying out cable, engines on stand-by, frequent position verification, pilot/tug availability.
7.3.9.2 Port closure updates.
7.3.10 Master accounts for deployed project/seismic/special equipment (ROV, submersibles, small boats) and liaises with Offshore Manager/Party Chief or DPA if in doubt.

chapters.title: Stability Guides
chapters.purpose: Critical operation guidelines to ensure the vessel remains within safe stability and stress limits at all times per the approved stability booklet and SOLAS II-1 Part B-1, covering responsibilities, loading computer tests, tank soundings, dry-docking, loss of stability actions and change of load line procedures.
key_requirements: 7.5.4 Master supervises ship's stability at all times and signs the vessel's stability information prior to sailing as approval of the sailing condition.
7.5.4 Chief Officer calculates and ensures stability and structural stresses are within stability booklet limits using accurate ballast, FW, fuel and lubricant quantities.
7.5.4 Calculates departure stability after cargo and bunkers; maintains stability calculation records.
7.5.4 Chief Officer tests the loading computer against Class-approved test data quarterly per maker's criteria and logs results.
7.5.4 Chief Engineer informs Master or Chief Officer before internal oil transfers and prior to bunkering.

7.5.5 Cargo operations incl. internal shifting conducted so adequate stability is maintained; load only to the load line mark for the zone during loading, passage and arrival allowing for consumption.

7.5.5 Free surface effect of slack tanks, including that generated by consumption during passage, taken into account; damage stability criteria verified for departure condition (intact compliance may not suffice).
7.5.5 Ability to withstand combined wind and wave rolling demonstrated for each loading condition and passage stage, especially RO/RO and car carriers.
7.5.5 Stability recalculated whenever a significant change in distribution of cargo, fuel, water or ballast is planned or made; draught, trim and list within booklet limits.
7.5.5 Before heavy weather, Master/Chief Officer minimise free surface from slack ballast tanks.
7.5.5 Chief Officer and Chief Engineer maintain daily soundings of ballast, FW and fuel tanks in sounding book/e-log, considering crew exposure when sounding manually.
7.5.6 Chief Officer/Master ensure adequate positive stability, upright condition and trim per dock requirements when entering dry dock.

7.5.7 Loading computer tested at least quarterly and/or after each loading; recorded in PMS and filed in Chief Officer's Ship Stability Calculations File G4; without loadicator, checks against standard conditions logged.
7.5.7 Errors reported immediately to vessel manager.
7.5.8 Shipyard recalculates stability and supplies a new stability booklet after every major structural modification.
7.5.9 Angle of loll corrected by ballasting low-side bottom tanks first; ballasting high side first is dangerous.
7.5.9 Damaged/aground actions consider SF/BM limits, GM with free surface, safe shifting of cargo/ballast/bunkers; obtain Company/Class ERS advice.
7.5.10 Vessels with multiple load lines inform Company/Vessel Manager on change at Owner/Charterer request and comply with flag/class instructions.
7.5.10 Safety standards maintained for maximum draught regardless of deadweight in use.
7.5.10 Only one set of load line marks visible with corresponding certificate in use; other marks painted out and unused certificates kept sealed under lock and key by Master.
7.5.10 New summer freeboard physically measured each side on every change and recorded in Deck Log Book and Official Log Book endorsed by Master; marks changed before loading at a loading port.

7.5.10 Change of marks witnessed by RO/Class where flag requires (or under Master's responsibility with Administration/RO approval and notification, surveyed at next port); Class endorses certificate.
7.5.10 Change recorded in deck logbook; shore updates Q88.
7.5.10 Apply load line of changed zone/season mid-voyage; at borderline harbours apply zone sailed through before/after; comply with marks regardless of trim, hogging or sagging.

Ensure minimal free surface before heavy weather; dry-dock stability

chapters.title: Launching, Maintenance and Testing Of Lifeboats (and Rescue Boats)
chapters.purpose: Ensures crew understand and comply with operational and safety guidelines for lifeboats and rescue boats, increasing readiness, reducing risk of mis-operation of critical components, building safe drill practices and meeting mandatory maintenance and testing requirements. Classified as a CRITICAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.6.4 Reference must be made to the SOLAS Training Manual, LSA Maintenance Record (BD13) or electronic PMS, manufacturer's manuals, Flag State guidelines and Risk Assessment guidelines (Ch.9.3)
7.6.4 Stricter Flag State guidance prevails.
7.6.5 Master ensures all crew are trained in lifeboat duties before participating in any lifeboat/rescue boat operation; training material current; drills at specified intervals.
7.6.5 Master ensures all lifeboat certification is up to date.
7.6.5 Master ensures mandated shore-personnel (authorised service provider) maintenance is done and certified.
7.6.5 Chief Officer, Chief Engineer and Third Officer ensure onboard inspection, testing and maintenance follow schedule, renewable items are renewed on time and boats are ready for immediate use
7.6.5 Deficiencies corrected without delay.

7.6.6 Boat maintenance is a priority item: never postponed, never hastily done; LSA Maintenance Manual inspection/maintenance guidelines strictly followed; spares ordered in good time from reputable suppliers.

7.6.6 Special attention to lifting/lowering components and hook release mechanisms; ship's staff shall never assume the role of authorised maintenance personnel for the annual and 5-yearly maintenance of these items.
7.6.6 Damage rendering a boat less than seaworthy is reported to Managers and Classification Society; repairs done to Class satisfaction.

7.6.6 Whenever anyone enters a lifeboat for maintenance/inspection, additional securing (hanging-off pendants, chain blocks) must be employed as decided by the Chief Officer, and removed/stowed immediately afterwards.

7.6.7 Boat drills (mustering, swinging out, launching and recovery, or simulated launching for free-fall boats) are carried out at SOLAS-prescribed intervals per the ship-specific SOLAS Training Manual
7.6.7 Crew participation has priority over other tasks.
7.6.7 Each lifeboat is launched and manoeuvred in the water by its assigned operating crew at least once every three months during an abandon ship drill
7.6.7 If port/operational restrictions prevent this, Master approaches Managers/Owners.
7.6.7 Before lowering, an Officer must ascertain the on-load/off-load release mechanism and hook positions are correct; only the minimum operating crew are aboard during lowering
7.6.7 Remaining crew embark via pilot ladder/safe means once the boat is in the water.
7.6.7 On recovery: hoist momentarily clear of water and reset hydrostatic interlocks; stop at 1-2 m above water and examine hooks
7.6.7 Operating crew disembark via embarkation ladders before boat is hoisted to stowed position.
7.6.7 If Fall Preventer Devices (FPDs) are used, strict procedures incl. warning notices and training must be in place (SOLAS TM Ch.6.7.1).

7.6.7 Free-fall boats launched per SOLAS TM with rescue boat in the water ready to assist; SOLAS relaxed intervals may be used but never exceeded. Rescue boats carry only operating crew when launched/hoisted
7.6.7 Rescued persons transferred to ship by safe means.
7.6.8 Ship Security Plan requirements followed to prevent stowaways in enclosed lifeboats; locking entrances is not encouraged, Company-supplied tell-tales are used instead.
7.6.9 Records: all drills in Deck Log Book; inspections/maintenance/renewals in LSA Maintenance Manual or electronic PMS (Chief Officer regularly checks entries)
7.6.9 Crew training on Forms D40/D41 and Personal Training Record Books.
7.6.9 External audit checklists/reports and corrective actions retained; undesired events involving boats reported in DOCMAP or Form DE45 with corrective/preventive measures.

Ensure drills are conducted at specified intervals in a safe and efficient manner
Ensure all lifeboat certification is up to date and mandated shore maintenance is done and certified

chapters.title: Mooring
chapters.purpose: Ensures all mooring operations (incl. tug, escort tug and line-boat work) are conducted safely with no harm to crew or terminal staff and no damage to vessel or terminal equipment. Classified as a SPECIAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.8.3 References: SOLAS II-1/3-8, MSC.1/Circ.1619, 1620, 1175 (and Rev.1), Mooring Line Management Plan (MLMP), COSWP, mooring/unmooring and brake test risk assessments; tankers also OCIMF/MEG.

7.8.4 Crew involved in mooring without STCW A-II/5 are trained by the Chief Officer; CBT #370 (Mooring risk assessment) and CBT #371 (Safe handling) completed; training/familiarisation records kept on board.
7.8.4 New/inexperienced seamen or cadets shall not handle ropes or wires in critical operations until trained (SSMM 6.1).

7.8.5 Entire mooring deck treated as snap-back area; entrance marked in yellow 'DANGER – SNAP BACK AREA'; alongside, ropes not left on winch drums; self-tensioning winches (tankers/ro-ro) not left in automatic mode.

7.8.6 Persons in charge fwd/aft are responsible to Master; ensure Risk Assessment hazards known and Toolbox Talk done; aft station informs bridge when propeller not clear; stations update bridge on clearances.
7.8.6 Chief Officer ensures mooring wires, ropes and equipment are maintained and protected from weather; certificates and change/renewal records documented.
7.8.7 Master collects information on the coming mooring from berth operator/pilot/agent; mooring plan: lines in same direction of same material/elasticity/tension, never mix synthetic and wire
7.8.7 Storm bollards used in strong wind; max one layer on tension side of split drums.

7.8.7 Each station supervised by a certified officer with a designated responsible person; two-way communication with bridge plus alternative means; routine Risk Assessment (SSMM 9.3) covering tugs/line boats
7.8.7 Pre-mooring toolbox talk on snap-back.

7.8.8 Winches/windlass tried out before operation; hydraulics warmed up in cold climates; defective lines not used; stations well lit, clean, free of oil; hazards highlighted; monkey fist rope-only, max 500 g.
7.8.8.1 PPE: safety helmet with chinstrap, gloves, safety boots, well-fitting overalls (SSMM 6.2).
7.8.9 Stoppers of same material as line, MBL about 50% of line MBL; no nylon stopper on nylon line; first two turns round first post then figure-eight on bitts.

7.8.9.1 Stay clear of lines under tension and snap-back zones; never stand on ropes or in bights; do not physically stop a line that takes charge; lines walked back not surged; protect from chafe and avoid sharp leads.
7.8.10.1 Master considers number/type/horsepower of tugs, bollard pull limits, connection method and communications; line-boat operations require communication, weather and payout limits
7.8.10.1 All tug/ancillary craft operations follow SSMM 9.3 risk assessment.
7.8.10.2 Officers in charge continuously monitor tow connection (no distraction such as signing tug receipts), use COSWP hand signals, make fast/let go only on bridge instruction.
7.8.10.2 Officers ensure tugs push at designated push points; bitt SWL marked and exceeds expected dynamic loads.
7.8.10.2 Bitt SWL marked and exceeds dynamic loads.
7.8.10.3 Escort tug positioning, emergency connection means and transit speed decided before transit; bollard pull/connection equipment communicated; direct mode 0-5 kn, indirect mode 5-12 kn.
7.8.11.1 Mooring line use documented in MLMP; inspection per maker recommendation recorded in PMS/MLMP; lines end-for-ended and retired per maker
7.8.11.1 New lines delivered with valid certificates marked with location and filed.
7.8.11.2 Brake bands/linings of winches/windlass inspected and recorded at intervals of max 6 months; spare linings carried; Slack/Heave directions marked; guards in place
7.8.11.2 Cargo vessels (excl. WASM) carry out annual brake rendering test and mark rendering point; tankers per MLMP/MEG.

7.8.11.3-11.5 Brake rendering test only where winches designed for it, with maker procedure and risk assessment/toolbox meeting; rendering set at not more than 60% of ship design MBL (1st layer, divided drums)
7.8.11.3-11.5 Record test parameters and mark date/force/pay-out direction on drum.
7.8.12 Moorings constantly attended during cargo ops/tide; Chief Officer writes precautions in port/cargo order book signed by duty officers and crew
7.8.12 Adjustments only with duty officer permission by min. two crew supervised by senior AB/bosun; fire-wires adjusted per terminal requirements.

Decide tug deployment (number, type, bollard pull, communications, push points) and inform officers in charge of tug locations and connection methods
Overall responsibility for safe mooring operations at fwd and aft stations

chapters.title: Preparation For Cargo Loading Operations
chapters.purpose: Lays down general guidelines for preparing the ship for cargo loading/discharging operations (ship-specific cargo operations manual to be consulted; see also SSMM 7.1 and 7.10 for cargo watch). Classified as a SPECIAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.9.3 Master and Chief Officer are responsible for ensuring the ship is ready in all respects to load/discharge the intended cargo; Chief Officer may delegate duties to the OOW and cargo crew.
7.9.4.1 On receipt of cargo particulars, Master and Chief Officer ascertain feasibility regarding type, nature, quantity, draft and weight distribution.
7.9.4.1 Master shall not agree to charterer demands for excessive deck loads, overloading or reduced reserve bunker margins; unreasonable demands reported to Company/owners.

7.9.4.2 Cargo tanks/holds thoroughly cleaned for the intended cargo, referring to Thomas Stowage, Yellow Book, and for tankers/gas/chemical ships Dr Verwey's tank cleaning guide, ISGOTT, SIGTTO and ICS guides.
7.9.4.2 All essential cargo equipment and systems checked and tested (where applicable) and kept ready.
7.9.4.2 Ship-provided cargo hoses must be fit for purpose, clearly marked, colour coded, with inspections/tests recorded in the vessel PMS.
7.9.4.3 Chief Officer ascertains all compartments to be loaded are in a safe condition to receive cargo.
7.9.4.3 Pre-arrival notifications sent to coastal state, port authorities, coast guard, agents and QI (tankers/gas carriers) as appropriate.
7.9.4.4 Crew briefed on loading/discharging with special reference to safety; hazardous cargo data sheets posted on notice boards.
7.9.4.5 Mandatory surveys/inspections conducted with terminal representatives, surveyors, cargo inspectors and charterers' representatives.
7.9.4.5 Ship/shore safety checklist completed and information exchanged; on tankers mutual safety examinations, loading/discharge rates and tank configuration explained
7.9.4.5 Emergency shutdown procedures agreed (tankers/gas carriers).
7.9.4.6 On dry cargo ships Chief Officer ensures hold bilges are cleaned and dry before every loading, previous cargo residues removed, strum box inspected; bilge inspections recorded in PMS
7.9.4.6 High level alarms tested where fitted.
7.9.4.7 Cargo checked against the Manifest to determine suitability for carriage and reject unsuitable items.

chapters.title: Safety During Cargo Operations
chapters.purpose: Ensures cargo operations are conducted safely and familiarises watchkeeping personnel with the risks and precautions of keeping a cargo watch (load distribution, stability, securing, dangerous goods, fire and pilferage). Classified as a SPECIAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.10.3 Master (directly or through Chief Officer) ensures cargo watch arrangements suit the cargo and a qualified deck officer supervises the cargo watch.
7.10.3 A 'Notification List' with contact numbers (CSO, PFSO, local fire brigade, port, agents, Company, local P&I correspondent) is prepared and prominently posted on board.
7.10.3 Duty officer keeps the cargo watch per Ch.7.1 and follows special instructions of Master/Chief Officer.
7.10.4 All deck officers and crew are briefed on cargo type, nature and safety precautions before cargo operations.
7.10.7 Master and Chief Officer ensure load distribution at all stages is within the ship's stability particulars
7.10.7 Stability, draft, trim, stresses and concurrent ballast operations within allowable limits and recorded as required by Master; deck/hold load density limits not exceeded.
7.10.7 On bulk carriers the ship/shore checklist is used before loading with agreement on loading rate, runs and hold-wise distribution.
7.10.8 Loads on cargo gear must not exceed SWL per plans/certificates; protective guards in place; equipment checked and tested before use
7.10.8 Duty officer checks for structural damage and reports it to stevedores/terminal immediately.
7.10.8 On tankers, safety cut-outs, alarms and associated devices are tested and results recorded in the relevant logbooks.

7.10.9 Chief Officer maintains adequate positive stability at all times; list, trim and draught kept safe with regard to squat, permissible depth, weather and load line zones; free surface effect minimised.
7.10.10 All personnel wear PPE appropriate to the activity (Ch.6.2); gangway and gangway net securely rigged (Ch.7.1); no walking/standing under suspended loads.

7.10.11 Duty officer ensures cargo is properly stowed and lashed per the Cargo Securing Manual; IMO Grain Rules applied for grain cargoes; container ships keel laid on/after 1 Jan 2015 carry a Cargo Safe Access Plan.
7.10.11 In US waters (to 12 nm) losses or jettisons of cargo are reported to the nearest Coast Guard Sector Office with what/how many/when/where/how details.

7.10.12 Before loading dangerous cargoes refer to MSDS and IMDG Code; IMDG segregation strictly followed; MFAG referred to as needed; Chief Officer ensures cargo space ventilation to prevent toxic gas accumulation.

7.10.13 Chief Officer and duty officers enforce 'No Smoking' around cargo spaces and decks; smoking only in designated areas; fire-fighting equipment ready and not obstructed by cargo; tankers follow ISGOTT.
7.10.13 In US ports a warning notice 'WARNING – DANGEROUS CARGO, NO VISITORS, NO SMOKING, NO OPEN LIGHTS' is displayed at gangway and bunker station facing seaward.
7.10.14 In suspect ports a roving patrol is maintained against pilferage; unauthorised persons not allowed on board.

chapters.title: Guidelines For The Inspection Of Tanks, Holds And Internal Structures
chapters.purpose: Specifies guidelines for the internal inspection, evaluation and recording of the condition of cargo holds, tanks, ballast tanks, void spaces and essential fittings (ref. MSC.215(82), MSC.1/Circ.1330). Classified as a SPECIAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.11.4 The Chief Officer inspects cargo tanks/holds, ballast tanks and associated fittings.
7.11.5 Ship arranges an internal tank inspection schedule in consultation with the Company (and coating manufacturer requirements) and enters it in the PMS.
7.11.5 Oil-major intervals: gas carriers - cargo tanks at drydock (max 60 months), hold spaces max 12 months, ballast/void/cofferdam 8-10 months
7.11.5 Crude/chemical tankers - cargo tanks at drydock (max 30 months), ballast/void 8-10 months; clean product tankers - cargo tanks 12 months, ballast/void 8-10 months.
7.11.5 Cargo tanks also inspected whenever gas free; gas carriers assess inspection frequency on age/type, yard, last drydock, experience, cargo hazards and operating environment
7.11.5 Vessel Manager forwards Class inspection schedules to Master.
7.11.6 Tank inspection results recorded on PMS forms PM11 and PM12 (or approved electronic equivalent); DE13, DE14, DE17, DE52, PTW-01, PTW-02 used as applicable.

7.11.7 Enclosed space entry (Ch.7.1.2), hot work (7.1.4), cold work (7.1.3) and PPE (6.2) precautions apply; crew trained on BWTS chemicals hazards; procedures warn of inerted/gas-residue ballast tanks.

7.11.8.1 Inspect longitudinals, tank top, hopper/wing tanks, bulkheads, manhole edges, brackets, cross deck strips, corrosion prevention system, hatch coamings, ladders, valves, heating coils, piping and cabling.
7.11.8.1 Special attention to critical pipelines passing through tanks that could cause pollution or safety system failure (fuel, steam, CO2 lines).
7.11.8.1 Special attention to critical pipelines through tanks (fuel, steam, CO2).

7.11.8.1 Inspection report includes compartment plan with location of structural deterioration, corrosion/pitting/wastage, coating breakdown, leakages, condition of cargo equipment and sediment build-up.
7.11.8.1 Unguarded manholes/areas cordoned off with signs; risk assessment carried out and attached to Toolbox Talk (DE78).
7.11.8.2 Coating condition rated Good (minor spot rusting) / Fair (local breakdown, light rusting over 20%) / Poor (general breakdown over 20% or hard scale over 10%)
7.11.8.2 Thickness gauging at suspect areas if equipment provided.
7.11.8.2 Check ballast/fuel tank intermediate bulkheads for breach; check anodes against maker life; clean and inspect notches, welds, hatch corners and brackets for cracks
