7.28.4 HODs responsible for maintenance, testing and routine inspection of anchoring equipment per PMS.
7.28.5 All anchoring operations supervised by a responsible person using checklist B08.

7.28.6 Bridge team collects information: manoeuvring characteristics, equipment limits, swinging circle, weather/tide, shelter, traffic, depth and holding ground, position-fixing marks, crew experience.
7.28.6 Emergency departure procedures from the anchorage considered; toolbox talk and risk assessment reviewed before anchoring operation.
7.28.6 Toolbox talk and risk assessment reviewed before anchoring.
7.28.7 Before anchoring, bridge, anchor party and engine room share: method of approach, anchor to be used, water depth, final shackles, method (let go or walk back) and chain reporting method.
7.28.8 Cable length guide: favourable conditions 3 x depth + 90 m; rough weather 4 x depth + 150 m
7.28.8 Avoid anchoring in Beaufort 7 or above (if wind reaches BF7 main engine on standby, bridge and engine room at navigation level).
7.28.8 Safety swinging circle calculated from cable length, depth plus hawse pipe height and hawse-to-stern distance; centre at hawse pipe position on letting go or when anchor touched bottom
7.28.8 Reduce radius by safety margin for early dragging warning.

7.28.9 Dropping method: lower under power to about 5 m above bottom, brake on, gypsy declutched, then let go; walk-back preferred for anchors over 10 t, deep water or hard bottom; running-out speed limited to 5-6 m/s
7.28.9 Speed over ground near zero; brakes examined before removing lashings.
7.28.9 Do not drop anchor in depths above 80 m (design limit about 82 m / three shackles); Master checks Class windlass limitations; power supply and lighting checked in advance
7.28.9 B08 used prior arrival, on arrival, post anchoring and while at anchor.
7.28.9 On emergency departure/weighing: use propulsion/thrusters to relieve chain tension, stop heaving on significant tension, apply band brake immediately; follow maker's windlass instructions.

7.28.10 Deep water anchoring (>82.5 m) avoided as far as practicable and never in strong wind/current, insufficient clearance or unknown depth/bottom; exceeds IACS/maker windlass limits unless Class notation held.
7.28.11 After anchoring monitor holding and readjust brakes after cooling; draw swinging circle on ECDIS and check ENC for hazards
7.28.11 OOW makes repetitive B08 checks at defined intervals and records positions in the deck logbook; consider weighing/re-anchoring after extended stays.
7.28.12 Anchors ready for letting go on arrival/departure and in anchoring depths as contingency; lashings removed
7.28.12 In emergencies stop/reverse propulsion before letting go, use short stay (about 1:3 depth/cable) to slow vessel.

7.28.13 If dragging suspected or vessel leaves swinging circle: OOW reports to Master immediately, informs nearby vessels, orders engine room to start main engine urgently and crew to stand by at anchor station
7.28.13 Countermeasures include more chain, ballast, reduce trim and windage, use propulsion.
7.28.14 New/inexperienced crew not used on anchor equipment until trained; crew without STCW A-II/5 trained by Chief Officer; familiarisation recorded on D-41
7.28.14 Drills per DE64 matrix: emergency anchoring, emergency bitter end release, mooring equipment failure table-top exercise (bi-annually).
7.28.15 Anchoring drills recorded in Deck Logbook; training records held on board; anchor equipment/windlass maintenance recorded in PMS.

chapters.title: Embarkation and Disembarkation
chapters.purpose: Establishes procedures for the construction, installation, maintenance, inspection and survey of means of embarkation and disembarkation (accommodation ladders, gangways and pilot ladders), identifies associated risks and recommends PPE (MSC.1/Circ.1331, SOLAS V/23). Classified as a CRITICAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.31.3 Risk Assessment (DE54) for rigging means of access, accommodation ladder/gangway and pilot ladder.
7.31.4 Means of access sited clear of working areas and not under suspended loads; adequate lighting; lifebuoy with self-igniting light and buoyant lifeline ready nearby.

7.31.4 Accommodation ladder lowest platform not more than 600 mm above waterline in lightest seagoing condition; combination with pilot ladder via guarded platform; ladder securely attached to prevent overturning.
7.31.4 Each accommodation ladder/gangway marked at each end with a plate showing max/min angles of inclination, design load, maximum load on bottom end plate and max operational load if less.
7.31.4 Gangways not used above 30 deg and accommodation ladders not above 55 deg from horizontal unless designed for it; gangways never secured to guardrails; gaps in bulwark fenced
7.31.4 Safety net rigged under accommodation ladders and gangways.
7.31.4 New accommodation ladders static load tested at maximum working load on installation; winch tested with at least two hoisting/lowering cycles.
7.31.4 Secondary means of support for Australian ports require Management of Change: risk assessed, procedures documented, PMS maintenance and crew training.

7.31.4 Accommodation ladders, gangways, winches and fittings maintained and inspected monthly (or per maker); additional checks for distortion, cracks and corrosion each time rigged; bent stanchions replaced
7.31.4 Guard ropes renewed when worn; moving parts greased.

7.31.4 Support wires renewed at intervals not exceeding 5 years; undersides examined regularly; all inspections/maintenance recorded in PMS with inspection date, inspector, next due date and wire renewal dates.
7.31.4 Annual survey examination of ladder steps, platforms, pivots, suspension points, stanchions, handrails, davit, wires, sheaves, gangway treads/stringers, winch brake, remote control and motor
7.31.4 Five-yearly operational load test with renewal survey.
7.31.4 At anchorage/underway embarkation: helmet, gloves, safety shoes, lifejacket, no luggage carried; sea limitation waves not more than 4 times service boat draft.
7.31.5 Pilot ladders manufacturer-certified to SOLAS; tagged/permanently marked for identification; PMS record of date placed in service and repairs.
7.31.5 Rigging per Pilot Transfer Arrangements booklet (SOLAS V/23, IMO A.1045(27)); 'Required Boarding Arrangements for Pilot' poster displayed on bridge
7.31.5 Ladder secured to strong point with shackles, deck tongue method prohibited; mechanical pilot hoists not used.
7.31.5 Pilot ladder manropes renewed at least every five years or earlier if deteriorated.
7.31.5 Crew rigging/supervising pilot ladders trained (D41 familiarisation, video 'Safe Set-up of Pilot Ladders').
7.31.5 Pilot ladder checks: clean and free of wear, spreaders equally spaced, steps horizontal/unpainted, retrieval line above lowest spreader leading forward, correct height above water.
7.31.5 Pilot ladder level with hull and secured to deck strong point (not railing); handhold stanchions present; sufficient illumination, lifebuoy and heaving line ready.

chapters.title: Operation in Cold Climate and Ice
chapters.purpose: Applies to all ships navigating in cold climate (below -10 C or equipment design limits), in or near ice-bound areas; sets out preparation, risk assessment, navigation and equipment precautions (Polar Code areas per the approved Polar Water Operation Manual). Classified as a CRITICAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.33.4 Master with Vessel Manager prepares the ship before cold climate/ice navigation

7.33.4 Operational risk assessment defines conditions, hazards, required capabilities and additional measures, and a ship/voyage specific checklist DE49 is prepared (Winterization class notation may substitute).

7.33.4 Master ensures all officers and crew are familiar with cold climate/ice precautions per the Mariners Handbook; local guidance sought from port agent/pilot service and Sailing Directions in ice-bound ports.
7.33.5 References: NP100 Mariners Handbook, Sailing Directions, IMO Polar Waters Guidelines, local ice guidelines, B11 Navigation in Ice checklist, DE49 checklist, Stability Booklet.
7.33.6 Vessel not to enter ice unless suitably strengthened/ice classed; an Ice Advisor does not relieve the Master of responsibility; unreported ice reported to shore weather authorities.
7.33.6 Avoid night navigation in ice and prefer longer open water routes; sharp lookout by all means (radar, searchlights, visual); constant communication when following an icebreaker.

7.33.6 Ensure sufficient residual stability where deck icing may occur and manoeuvre to reduce spray icing; non-ice-class vessels seek office/local ice expert advice and inform underwriters in advance.
7.33.6 Golden rules in ice: keep moving, work with ice movement, avoid excessive speed, right-angle approach to floes, rudder amidships before sternway, avoid anchoring in moving close pack ice.

7.33.6 In port: check ice thickness, forecast and port closure via agent; verify icebreaker/tug capability; avoid astern engine and bow thruster in ice except emergency; discuss departure plan with pilot
7.33.6 Ensure propeller immersion below ice thickness.
7.33.6 Exposed deck lines protected or fully drained; if fire lines isolated/drained, crew familiar and drilled in section valve locations and rapid re-pressurisation.

7.33.6 Slippery decks, ramps and gangways cordoned off or treated; hydraulic systems warmed in good time; ice accumulation safely removed for stability; appropriate cold weather clothing worn with sufficient stock.
7.33.6 Use low sea chest inlets with steam/compressed air to prevent ice build-up; lifesaving equipment kept ice-free and ready; emergency battery rooms kept at temperature for required capacity.
7.33.6 Crew drill before entering cold climate covering entrapment in ice, damage control and cold water survival.
7.33.6 Salt water ballast used to avoid freezing; ballast tank sounding pipes sounded frequently, steam injection/anti-freeze considered
7.33.6 Radar scanners rotating continuously, bridge heaters on, wipers operated periodically.

3/O: As OOW maintain sharp lookout for ice; keep lifesaving equipment ice-free and ready

chapters.title: Refugees
chapters.purpose: Provides guidance on handling refugees/migrants picked up at sea during SAR operations, including notifications, crew preparation, safe embarkation, control and welfare on board, port arrival formalities and post-disembarkation actions. Classified as a SPECIAL OPERATION (Ch.3.1).
key_requirements: 7.38.3 References: IMO/Flag circulars, UNHCR guidelines, CSO updates, ICS Large Scale Rescue at Sea, NSA Migrants at Sea, and the Vessel Contingency Manual for reporting procedures.
7.38.5 Master makes relevant log entries and informs the Company, next port agents (circumstances and number of refugees) and the P&I club.
7.38.5 Crew prepared in advance: scenarios, roles, risks discussed with reference to vessel-specific recovery of persons from water procedures (SOLAS TM Ch.17.2).

7.38.5 Approach with MOB/rescue boat, provide life vests, water and nutrition; establish trust and calm refugees; use own ship to shelter their boat; keep in touch with MRCC and maintain internal communication.
7.38.5 Before embarking: secure and prepare ship, lock interior, seal off dangerous areas; ensure safety and order during the critical transfer phase.
7.38.5 Record number of people with gender, children and nationality; document events.
7.38.5 Implement hygiene and infectious disease control measures; crew use protective gear.

7.38.5 Keep refugees on deck in a 24/7 controlled environment; crew in uniform displaying authority; control items brought aboard (body check/metal scan), confiscate knives; no ignition sources or open flames on deck.

7.38.5 Show cultural and gender sensitivity, identify and assist the most vulnerable, ensure supervision of (possibly unaccompanied) children; provide water, food, shelter and medical aid per vessel capability
7.38.5 Consider destroying the refugee boat.
7.38.5 Confirm arrival port agent informs port authorities, immigration, UNHCR local office and Flag State consulate and requests permission to enter port.

7.38.5 After disembarkation: search for stowaways, hand over remaining ID papers/belongings to authorities, disinfect decks/areas, dispose of used PPE properly, debrief crew with extra follow-up as needed.

chapters.title: Emergency Drills And Training
chapters.purpose: Sets objectives, minimum schedules (weekly to annual, incl. flag-specific), procedures for key drills (abandon ship, fire, security, anti-pollution, enclosed space, MES) and record/evaluation requirements for shipboard emergency drills and training under ISM Code 8 and SOLAS III/19 & 30.

8.2.3 All on board participate and absentees with reasons recorded in the log book.
8.2.3 Passenger vessels: weekly abandon ship and fire drill; each crew member participates in both at least monthly; Master informs Company if launching intervals cannot be met.
8.2.4 Drill schedules in DE64 (all vessels), DE64A (tankers/gas) and CVDE64 (cruise)
8.2.4 Additional flag requirements complied with (e.g. weekly watertight door drill Liberia/Marshall Islands, fortnightly abandon ship/fire drill Malta, quarterly MOB Malta/Marshall Islands).

8.2.4 BI-ANNUALLY: grounding, collision, serious injury/death, propulsion/steering failure, blackout recovery, cargo spillage, MOB/recovery of person, heavy weather damage, flooding.

chapters.title: Undesired Events
chapters.purpose: Defines accidents, near accidents, non-conformities and hazard observations and sets the process for reporting (Docmap / DE45), root cause analysis, loss recording, correction/corrective/preventive action, closure timeframes and audit/inspection reporting (ISM Code 9).
key_requirements: 9.1.1 All incidents reported in Docmap (or form DE45 where Docmap not fitted); incidents classed as Accidents (event with loss), Near Accidents (event without loss) and Non-Conformities (non-fulfilment of a requirement).

9.1.1 Hazard observations (unsafe acts and unsafe conditions) are reported; incidents are investigated by the DPA or a suitably qualified person and analysed for correction and corrective action per GIMS procedures.
9.1.2 Shipboard management performs a detailed analysis, followed by Company analysis for lessons learned
9.1.2 Root cause analysis identifies immediate causes, causal factors and root causes with recommendations at each level; analysis done in Docmap or DE45.
9.1.2.1 Immediate causes classified as substandard acts/practices (e.g. defeating safety devices, no PPE, improper lifting, using defective equipment).
9.1.2.1 Or substandard conditions (defective tools, poor housekeeping, inadequate ventilation, poor maintenance, inadequate barriers or PPE).
9.1.2.2-9.1.2.3 Causal factors: management, competence and individual factors; root causes: inadequate management system, inadequate compliance, inadequate standards.
9.1.3 Actual or envisaged loss (time, cost, harm to people, property, environment, process) recorded for each incident.
9.1.4 Correction (quick fix) distinguished from corrective action (removing causal factors, permanent fix) and preventive action (removing causes of potential incidents)
9.1.4 Restoring equipment to normal is not a corrective action; reference the procedure document where a procedural deficiency is the cause.
9.1.5 The Responsible Onboard (the Master, unless exception documented via Management of Change form DE55) / Safety Officer reports all incidents to the Company.
9.1.5 Reportable: accidents, near accidents, non-conformities, hazard observations and cyber incidents.
9.1.5 VCM Ch.4.1 incidents reported immediately, others as soon as practicable.

9.1.5 Flag/Port State mandatory reporting formats and timeframes followed; security incidents reported as Report of Security Incidents in Docmap or form S02; US-trading passenger vessels keep a separate CVSSA log book.
9.1.6 Incidents closed by the responsible person ashore once evidence of corrective/preventive action is provided: Low risk (1-4) within 3 months (90 days)
9.1.6 Medium (5-9) and High (10-25) as soon as practicable in consultation with management office; hazard observations may be closed by the Master.

9.1.6 Audit/inspection non-conformances corrected and closed within the timeframe set by external authorities or agreed with the internal auditor; observations closed before they deteriorate into non-conformances.
9.1.7 Audits/inspections reported as an Audit Inspection Report (AIR) in Docmap; internal audit AIR auto-created from e-audit
9.1.7 External audit (Flag, Class, PSC) AIR created by Responsible Onboard with a linked NC/Observation report for each finding; AIR closed only when all linked reports closed.

chapters.title: Toolbox Talk And Risk Assessment
chapters.purpose: Provides shipboard management with a tool to identify and control all risks of shipboard operations (routine, non-routine, maintenance, SIMOPS, changes) and reduce them to ALARP through risk assessment and toolbox talks before work starts.

9.3.4.3 Toolbox talk held before any work involving more than one person with risk to persons, property or environment; risk assessment discussed and control measures verified complete.
9.3.4.3 If no reviewed and approved risk assessment exists for the task, the task supervisor initiates a new one.

9.3.7 Control hierarchy priority: elimination, substitution, engineering controls (lock-out/isolation), signage/administrative controls, PPE.
9.3.7 Risk assessment is a team effort including as a minimum Head of Department(s) and the staff performing the activity; sufficient review time allowed and office input sought if required.

chapters.title: Fire Safety
chapters.purpose: Identifies common sources of shipboard fires and the associated preventive measures, fire patrols, detection systems, FFA upkeep and fire plans; applies to all vessels, with tankers additionally guided by ISGOTT.
key_requirements: 10.4.3.1 Smoking strictly prohibited outside designated smoking areas; only safety matches; matches/lighters banned outside accommodation; mechanical and electrical-ignition lighters prohibited on tankers.

10.4.3.2 Prevent oil on hot surfaces: sheaths on HP oil pipes, hot surfaces insulated, leaks rectified promptly, fire detection tested, galley vent ducts/grease traps cleaned, fire blanket and extinguisher in galley.
10.4.3.3 Electric motors, heaters and dryers regularly inspected; metal flanges bonded; tank cleaning hose continuity checked; portable lamps checked by electrician before use.
10.4.3.4 Manufacturer's operation and maintenance recommendations strictly observed to prevent overheating of bearings and seals.
10.4.3.5 Boiler smoke side and exhaust uptakes kept clean; deck duty officer informed to watch for funnel sparks during sootblowing; water drained from fuel tanks regularly.
10.4.3.7 Tankers suspend cargo operations, tank cleaning or gas freeing during electrical storms or when forecast.
10.4.3.8 Lithium batteries: use only designed batteries, avoid damage/short circuit, store used batteries separately and dry until landed; charging not left unattended unless in a designated space.
10.4.4.1 Strict cleanliness rules; no accumulation of waste material or unattended flammable spillages.
10.4.4.2 C/O and C/E responsible for arranging and supervising fire patrols; deck and engine watch members regularly inspect deck and machinery spaces; cargo space watches as required by cargo.

10.4.4.2 Daily at sea between 2000 and 0600 (2200 on cruise vessels) an instructed crew member (the signed-off look-out) patrols the vessel as instructed by the Duty Officer and reports results to the OOW.
10.4.4.2 Continuous fire patrols during major contractor repairs or drydock while work is in progress.
10.4.4.3 Fire safety placards and signs per Yellow Book clearly displayed at appropriate locations.
10.4.4.4 Regular fire drills at various ship locations to test and improve crew response.
10.4.4.5 All ventilators tested regularly and the spaces they serve clearly marked.
10.4.4.6 Enclosed space atmosphere tested for explosive gas, oxygen, toxic gas (and CO for coal-carrying bulkers) and Permit to Work obtained before entry (SSMM 7.1.2).
10.4.4.7 Fire detection/alarm systems regularly tested; log sheet posted adjacent to fire detection panels on Bridge and ECR recording all detector/system isolations including timer isolations.
10.4.5 C/E responsible for FFA upkeep/repairs and FFA Maintenance Record Book BE14, assisted by C/O/safety officer; automatic firefighting systems kept in automatic mode.
10.4.6 Fire plans positioned at strategic places and main accesses such as stern door and gangway.

chapters.title: Care And Test Of Measuring Instruments
chapters.rev: PD388 Version 8, 30/06/2016 (header printed as Operational Manual Cruise Vessel)
chapters.purpose: Confirms the operational status and accuracy of onboard testing/measuring instruments (especially gas detectors) before and during use, and keeps records of location, calibration checks and inventory with identified responsible persons.
key_requirements: 10.5.3 BD10-listed equipment calibrated at stated intervals against traceable standards: shore agencies, maker's method with test gas/piece, comparison with certified reference instrument, or certified specimen.

10.5.6 Instruments kept in a separate locker; sensors stored in silica-gel receptacle with tag when removed and date of first use marked on sensor.

10.5.8.2 Instruments checked and calibrated before use with correct calibration gas; O2 meter spanned with fresh air and zeroed with nitrogen (or 5% O2/95% N2 gas); never use lighter/propane gas.
10.5.8.2 Manufacturer correlation curves used when calibrating with a different gas; zero setting checked at frequent intervals during use.

chapters.title: Trading And Other Ship's Certificates
chapters.purpose: Establishes guidelines to ensure vessels carry valid, appropriate certificates for their type and trade in accordance with international and national requirements, with the Master responsible for validity and records.
key_requirements: 11.2.3 The Master is responsible for ensuring the ship's certificates are valid at all times.
11.2.4 All certificates carried onboard must be originals, except the Company's Document of Compliance (DOC), which may be a copy.

11.2.4 Electronic RO/Flag certificates accepted if valid, in convention format, protected from edits, with unique tracking number and printable verification symbol; RO verification instructions onboard.
11.2.4 Certificates for wires, ropes, slings, safety equipment and other Class-certified equipment carefully kept onboard and readily available for inspection.
11.2.4 Ship Sanitation Control (Exemption) Certificate issued only from an IHR-authorised port (check WHO list).
11.2.4 Master stores certificates in a dedicated folder under his safekeeping.
11.2.4 Record of ship's certificates maintained and updated at least monthly; copy kept in the certificate folder.
11.2.4 Form D-7 'Record of Ship's Certificates' completed and sent to the Company every month.
11.2.4 Certificates due for renewal highlighted for ready reference.
11.2.4 Latest class survey status report available onboard; surveys arranged with the Company well in time.
11.2.2 References: SOLAS Chapter I Part B, SSMM Ch. 12.1, FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2.

Master: Ensure all ship's certificates valid; keep originals in dedicated folder
Update certificate record monthly and send D-7 to Company monthly
Keep latest class survey status onboard and arrange surveys in time with Company
C/O: Keep certificates for wires, ropes, slings and safety equipment available for inspection
C/E: Keep certificates for engine-related Class-certified equipment available for inspection

chapters.title: Documentation Control
chapters.purpose: Establishes procedures to control all governing shipboard documents so that only current authorised versions are available, mandatory documents are carried, onboard-prepared instructions are approved before issue, and obsolete documents are removed.
key_requirements: 11.3.1 Only current versions of authorised documents available at all relevant locations; obsolete documents promptly removed from points of use.
11.3.2 Ship-specific instructions/procedures prepared onboard (including changes to emergency procedures) reviewed and approved by C/O, C/E or Master before issue/re-issue.
11.3.2 Onboard instructions marked with date of issue, name/rank/signature of authoriser, distribution/posting location and revision number.
11.3.2 Record of all ship-specific instructions and their locations maintained in the Yellow Book and included in Master's handover.
11.3.2 Master maintains a control list of posted instructions/standing orders/notices (date, subject, issuing authority, location) and hands it over to his relief.
11.3.2 All posted notices countersigned by the Master; Master informed of removal/replacement of notices.
11.3.3 Shore-prepared documentation approved by Company Documentation Committee; MfMs and VCM issued by each management centre; changes from previous revision shown in blue; TOC shows approval dates.
11.3.4 Master ensures manuals onboard are updated on receipt of new/revised documents, confirms receipt to Company on request, and discards obsolete documents.
11.3.4 Every Company manual has an attached sign sheet signed by specified personnel after familiarisation.
11.3.4 Master ensures all documents required for ship and trade are onboard per Yellow Book and mandatory requirements, and that Yellow Book checklists are made vessel-specific.
11.3.4 Plans/drawings amended after alterations to structure, machinery or fittings; changes to Class/Flag-approved documents authorised by those bodies.
11.3.4 Owners, charterers, surveyors and authorities may examine documentation with Master's permission, but copying or removal is strictly prohibited.
11.3.4 All Company manuals and unused forms returned to the Company when management is terminated.

Master: Approve onboard instructions; maintain and hand over control list of posted notices; countersign notices
Update manuals on revision, confirm to Company, discard obsolete documents; ensure mandatory documents and vessel-specific checklists onboard
Arrange amendment of plans after alterations; control examination/copying of documents
C/O: Review and approve ship-specific deck instructions/procedures before issue
C/E: Review and approve ship-specific engine instructions/procedures before issue
All: Sign manual familiarisation sign sheets; follow only current authorised documents

chapters.title: Records And Filing
chapters.purpose: Specifies the location, control, storage, retention, disposal/return and correction rules for shipboard records and the Company's filing systems.
key_requirements: 11.4.2 Each department head maintains all reports and records of his department; the Master's records and filing system are exclusively under his charge.
11.4.2 All personnel should know the location of required data and records.
11.4.2 Company-approved filing systems for Master, Chief Engineer and Chief Officer specified in the Yellow Book shall be followed.
11.4.2 Signed forms may be scanned and filed onboard; forms identified as e-filing may be kept as soft copy in the ship's common folder.
11.4.2 Computer-generated records backed up and stored in an alternate location, preferably a separate fire zone.
11.4.2 Master responsible for effective control of shipboard documentation, confidentiality and accountability.
11.4.2 Owners, charterers, surveyors and authorities may examine documentation with Master's permission; copying or removal strictly prohibited.
11.4.3 Records retained for periods prescribed in the Yellow Book unless contracts or statutory requirements specify otherwise.
11.4.4 All records are property of WSM and returned on termination of management unless instructed otherwise.
11.4.4 Sensitive/confidential documents destroyed by shredding or incineration at Master's discretion.
11.4.5 Never erase, use correction ink/tape, overwrite or make illegible any entry in a logbook or SMS documentation.

Master: Control all shipboard documentation, confidentiality and accountability; own filing system per Yellow Book
Permit examination but prevent copying/removal; decide destruction of confidential documents
C/O: Maintain deck department records and Chief Officer filing system per Yellow Book
C/E: Maintain engine department records and Chief Engineer filing system per Yellow Book
All: Know location of required records; back up computer records; never erase or overwrite logbook/SMS entries

chapters.title: Log Entries
chapters.purpose: Sets the procedure for making factual, timely and properly corrected entries in ship's logbooks, referencing the booklet 'Master's Role in Collecting Evidence'.
key_requirements: 11.5.1 Refer to the booklet 'Master's Role in Collecting Evidence' in the ship's library for the importance of log entries.
11.5.2.1 Make a log entry as soon as an event occurs and in no case later than the end of the watch.
11.5.2.1 Log entries state only facts as events occur, not opinions of the person making the entry.
11.5.2.1 Transfer entries accurately to the ship's logbook if a draft (rough) logbook is kept.
11.5.2.1 Fill in all details illustrating the circumstances of an incident or damage, such as weather conditions.
11.5.2.1 Logbooks signed by the officer or engineer at the end of each watch.
11.5.2.1 Follow the instructions specified in the logbooks when making entries.
11.5.2.1 Correct errors by a single line through the entry with the correct entry written next to it, initialled by the person making the change.
11.5.2.1 Obtain Master's approval before presenting the logbook for inspection by anyone other than the Company.
11.5.2.1 In case of accidents, log entries made only after the Master has consented to the wording.

Master: Approve logbook presentation to third parties; consent to wording of accident entries
C/O: Make timely factual entries and sign deck logbook at end of watch
2/O: Make timely factual entries and sign deck logbook at end of watch
3/O: Make timely factual entries and sign deck logbook at end of watch
C/E: Ensure engine logbook entries are factual, timely and signed each watch
2/E: Make timely factual entries and sign engine logbook at end of watch
3/E: Make timely factual entries and sign engine logbook at end of watch
All: Never erase; correct with single line and initials; record facts not opinions

chapters.title: Log Extracts
chapters.purpose: Defines when verbatim log extracts must be sent to the Company (in addition to the DE45 incident report) and how they are signed and retained.
key_requirements: 11.6.1 Log extracts are a verbatim record of the original logbook entry, including punctuation.
11.6.1 Log extracts sent to the Company duly signed and stamped by the Master and heads of department, in addition to form DE45 incident report.
11.6.1 Log extract required for any injury to persons and all cases of death onboard.
11.6.1 Log extract required on collision or contact with other craft/vessels (tugs, pilot boats, fishing boats) or damage to shore installations or fairway marks.
11.6.1 Log extract required when assisting tugs damage own ship or third party property, or when ship's gear (anchors, booms, moorings, ramps, cranes) damages third party property.
11.6.1 Log extract required in all cases of actual or suspected pollution by the ship (oil, sewage, garbage).
11.6.1 Log extract required when damage to own ship/equipment is caused by non-crew (e.g. stevedores) or when cargo is damaged or significantly deficient.
11.6.1 Log extract required for theft from ship's stores/equipment and whenever stowaways are found onboard.
11.6.1 Log extract required for loss of lubricants, bunkers, provisions or stores in connection with an average, and for damage involving general or particular average repairs.
11.6.1 Log extract required when damage cannot be assessed due to location (bottom, heavy weather, ice) or when an accident causes delay in port or voyage prolongation.
11.6.2 A copy of each log extract retained onboard as described in Yellow Book Ch.1 Sec.3.

Master: Sign and stamp log extracts and send to Company with DE45; ensure retention onboard
C/O: As HOD sign log extracts for deck events (injury, collision, cargo damage, pollution, stowaways)
C/E: As HOD sign log extracts for engine events (pollution, bunker/lubricant loss, machinery damage)
All: Officers ensure original log entries are accurate since extracts must be verbatim

chapters.title: Management Of Change
chapters.purpose: Puts in place formal change management procedures so that temporary or permanent changes to equipment, personnel, operating conditions, procedures, contractors or new vessels are risk assessed and controlled before, during and after the change.
key_requirements: 11.7.1 All changes affecting routine and non-routine tasks must undergo a risk assessment to identify hazards and reduce operational risk.
11.7.3 Formal MOC required for any transition of people, process or machinery where no documented procedure exists; MOC not required where a documented procedure already covers the change.
11.7.4 MOC process follows form/checklist DE55 and must be authorised by the Master.

11.7.4 Step 1: identify what is changed (equipment/chemicals, tasks, workplace, workforce/organisation, responsibility, vessel design, new vessel type, technology incl. cyber risk, third-party contractors).
11.7.4 Steps 2–3: specify why the change is necessary with safety/environmental implications, and when it takes effect, its duration and whether permanent, planned or enforced.
11.7.4 Steps 4–5: identify adverse effects on safety, environment, operations, rules, SMS and security, and hazards during implementation (e.g. hot work, generator shutdown, biological agents).
11.7.4 Step 6: where hazards are found, a DE54 risk assessment is carried out; if risk cannot be reduced to acceptable, the change cannot proceed.
11.7.4 Step 7: record MOC team members (including Master) and who requires training as a result of the change.
11.7.4 Steps 8–10: Vessel/Fleet Manager reviews Master's request, HSEQ analyses hazards and SMS conflicts (Class/authorities consulted if needed); approval by General Manager or HSEQ Manager.
11.7.4 Step 11: VM enters earliest implementation date, MOC closure due date and effectiveness evaluation date and returns form to vessel.
11.7.4 Step 12: Master notifies all affected persons, effects the change, records completion date, ensures training, amends drawings/instructions/procedures and includes change in handover notes.
11.7.4 Step 13: effectiveness monitored and recorded in DE55 by the VM's date; process repeated if not effective.
11.7.5 Emergency changes may be made without prior DE55 provided a quick risk assessment and mitigation are done; DE55 recorded retroactively.

11.7.5 MOC applies e.g. to new/modified machinery, major structural changes, new regulations, equipment/procedure failure, lessons learned, manning changes, new cargo products; deviations approved by office.
11.7.6 SMS change suggestions sent to HSEQ manager via SMS Review minutes, Safety Committee meetings or DocMap Improvement Suggestion; SMS changes needing RA follow DE55.
11.7.7 Master forwards a copy of all revised shipboard drawings/documents to the manager's office.
11.7.8 Master requests review and revalidation of approvals if changes are not carried out within the proposed time scale.

Master: Authorise DE55 MOC requests; notify affected persons; implement change, training, document amendments and handover notes
Forward revised drawings/documents to office; request revalidation if change delayed; monitor effectiveness
C/O: Participate in MOC team and DE54 risk assessment for deck changes; identify training needs
C/E: Participate in MOC team and DE54 risk assessment for machinery/equipment changes; identify training needs
All: Follow changed procedures after briefing/training; raise improvement suggestions via DocMap; mention changes in handover notes

chapters.title: Audits, Surveys, Inspections And Reports
chapters.purpose: Identifies the shipboard audits, surveys and inspections (internal, Class/Flag, statutory, vetting, Vessel Manager, Flag State, PSC) and gives guidelines for their scheduling, preparation, execution, reporting in Docmap/D55 and follow-up of findings.
key_requirements: 12.1.2 Master ensures all required audits, surveys and inspections are done within the required time frame in consultation with the Vessel Manager; HODs manage pre/post activities in their departments.
12.1.2 C/E, if authorised, conducts and follows up Continuous Survey of Machinery (CMS); Master arranges approval of results by authorities.
12.1.5 Master informs the Company as soon as possible if the vessel cannot meet a scheduled audit/survey/inspection.
12.1.6 Preparation: assign tasks and brief personnel, prepare spares/tools/documents, test systems beforehand, provide safe access/lighting/PPE; machinery survey items cleaned, laid out and labelled.
12.1.7 Visitors escorted by the relevant HOD or designated officer; only the liaison officer answers queries; HOD returns affected systems to normal status afterwards.

12.1.7.1 Internal audits by HSEQ-approved auditor at intervals not exceeding 12 months (max +3 months in exceptional circumstances with risk assessment); new vessels within 3 months, before RO initial audit.

12.1.7.1 Internal audit scope covers Company documentation, ISM/MLC/ISPS, ISO 9001/14001/50001, statutory/Flag/Class rules; may include navigational audit, cargo audit, VGP, pre-PSC and pre-vetting inspections.
12.1.7.1 Minor NCs and observations closed within 90 days; major NCs within 30 days; extension formally requested by Master to HSEQ Manager; number of audits/NCs reported in Weekly Report D55.

12.1.7.2 All Class/Flag audits reported in Weekly Report D55 and Docmap; Audit and Inspection Report (AIR) created per audit with findings as individual linked reports; report e-mailed to VM and HSEQ Manager.
12.1.7.2 Suggestions for Improvement and Noteworthy Efforts entered in Docmap linked to the AIR and discussed at the Safety Committee Meeting.
12.1.7.3 CSM schedule/status tabulated on Form E8; survey documentation (DE14 + E15) forwarded to Vessel Manager; any defect leading to NC, CC or CA reported in Docmap.

12.1.7.4 External inspections (Oil Majors, CDI, RightShip, charterers, insurers) reported in Docmap as AIR, flawless or not; Master e-mails report to VM/FM/HSEQ cc vettingreport@wilhelmsen.com (NIL too).
12.1.7.4 If Master disagrees with vetting findings, point out politely and inform Company; proposed corrective actions sent within the vetting regime timeline for operator comments.
12.1.7.5 Vessel Manager inspection (RD03) at least 2 per 12 months (tankers/gas carriers max 6-month interval); closing meeting held; NCs closed within 90 days and reported in Docmap and D55.

12.1.7.6 Annual Flag State safety inspection for Liberia, Panama, Marshall Islands and Bahamas vessels; all FSIs reported in Docmap as AIR and D55; Panama: corrections reported within 30 days on F-IASI-01-01.

12.1.7.7 All PSC inspections, flawless or with deficiencies, reported in Docmap as AIR with categorised deficiencies and in D55; Master e-mails report to VM/FM/HSEQ with copy to PSCReport@wilhelmsen.com.

12.1.7.7 Flag PSC reporting: Panama (psc@amp.gob.pa, F253 + crew list), Liberia (report within 48 h, CAR within 7 days on RLM-031, immediate detention notice), Cayman (7 days), Cyprus/MI (detention), Bahamas (Form A/B).
12.1.7.8 NIR (Paris/Tokyo/Black Sea/IOMOU): pre-arrival notification 72 h for expanded-inspection ships (high risk or passenger/tanker/gas/chemical/bulk over 12 yrs), 24 h for others, plus ATA/ATD.

Master: Ensure audits/surveys/inspections done on time; inform Company if schedule cannot be met
Report every audit, FSI, PSC and vetting inspection in Docmap (AIR) and Weekly Report D55; e-mail reports to VM/FM/HSEQ and flag as required
Request NC closure extensions from HSEQ Manager; challenge vetting findings politely and inform Company
C/O: Manage pre/post audit-survey-inspection activities for deck; escort and liaise with surveyors; return systems to normal; rectify shortcomings
C/E: Conduct/follow up CSM if authorised and maintain Form E8; forward DE14/E15 to VM; manage engine survey preparation and rectification of findings
2/E: Prepare machinery survey items cleaned, laid out and labelled; assist C/E with CSM
All: Cooperate with auditors/inspectors; prepare assigned items; close NCs within 90 days (minor) / 30 days (major); discuss SFIs at Safety Committee

chapters.title: Shipboard Management Systems Review
chapters.purpose: Defines the Shipboard Management Systems Review (SMSR) by which the Master and HODs evaluate the effectiveness of the shipboard SMS and feed suggestions for continual improvement to the Company.
key_requirements: 12.2.3 Master with heads of department conducts an SMSR during his tenure and submits it at least one month before signing off, so the Company can respond while he is still onboard.
12.2.3 Where the Master's contract is extended, SMSR done at intervals not exceeding 12 months.
12.2.3 SMSR submitted via the Docmap observation module (Form D48 for vessels without Docmap).
12.2.3 Navigational audit conducted as part of the SMSR using form D42 (SMSR Checklist); non-conformances followed up in Docmap.
12.2.3 Form D42A 'Navigational Assessment Checklist' completed for vessels subject to TMSA/OVMSA/RISQ (may be applied to other vessels).
12.2.3 Remarks from D42 transferred to the 'Summary of remarks from D42' section and D42/D42A attached to the SMSR report.
12.2.4 Master ('Responsible Onboard') and HODs complete SMSR with supporting documents and forward to Vessel Manager; Suggestion For Improvement created in Docmap for SMS changes.
12.2.4 Workflow: VM reviews/hearing, HSEQ Manager evaluates (SMS changes to Document Committee), Fleet Manager approves/rejects; GM notified of concerns; completed SMSR viewable onboard.
12.2.4 Exceptions to the Master being Responsible Onboard documented with Management of Change form DE55; observation entries created in Docmap for any NCs.
12.2.5 Review evaluates how well SMS documentation works onboard incl. safety, security (incl. cyber), maintenance and environmental procedures, with improvement suggestions.
12.2.5 ISO 14001 vessels not in office program set and monitor their own environmental aspects/objectives based on the EC environmental program.

12.2.5 Review items: compliance challenges, crew proficiency, owner/charterer conflicts, PSC/flag experience, documentation, policy adherence, training needs, audits, suppliers, ISO status, Docmap status, D42/D42A.

Master: Conduct and submit SMSR one month before sign-off (or every 12 months); complete D42 navigational audit and D42A where applicable; submit via Docmap
Create SFIs for SMS changes; review open Docmap observations; assess crew proficiency and training needs
C/O: Participate in SMSR as HOD; contribute deck/navigation input to D42/D42A and improvement suggestions
C/E: Participate in SMSR as HOD; contribute maintenance/environmental/energy input
All: Officers and crew demonstrate familiarity with and adherence to Company policy, reviewed in the SMSR

chapters.title: ISM Certification
chapters.purpose: States the applicability of ISM certification to the fleet and the Master's responsibility for keeping a copy of the DOC and a valid SMC onboard and maintained through the required audits.
key_requirements: 13.1 ISM Code applies to passenger ships (from 1 July 1998), tankers/gas carriers/bulk carriers/cargo HSC of 500 GT and above (by 1 July 1998) and other cargo ships and MODUs of 500 GT and above (by 1 July 2002).
13.2 The Master is responsible for ensuring the ISM certification requirements are satisfied.
13.3 A copy of the Company's valid Document of Compliance (DOC) shall be onboard and produced by the Master to authorised inspectors/auditors on request.
13.3 A valid Safety Management Certificate (SMC) issued in the vessel's name by the Administration or RO shall be onboard and maintained per the ISM Code.
13.3 To maintain SMC validity the vessel undergoes annual internal audits and an external intermediate audit within 2.5 years (+/- 6 months) of the SMC issue date.
13.3 Serious deficiencies in the ship's SMS may cause the SMC to be voided by the issuing authority.
13.4 References: ISM Code and Flag State regulations (YB 4.1), SOLAS Chapter IX.

Master: Keep DOC copy and valid SMC onboard; produce DOC on request; ensure annual internal audits and intermediate external audit are carried out
